_doc: The Regulars (core/regulars.gd): recurring characters. home: the town they live in (an NPC all the time; or zone + npc: a home resident who is the Regular, no NPC spawned); away: a second town where they turn up once favour is 2; likes: the item that wins them over; intro / meet / letter / offer / chat / thanks: the lines for each beat ({player} is you). Flag reg_<id> holds {favour, pts, gift_day, met, letter, manager}.

regulars.name: Ned Corrigan
regulars.hint: Ned says a haddock, fresh, is the only conversation he needs.
intro: A man in a yellow oilskin is sitting on a bollard, staring at the harbour as though it owes him money.
Ned: Thirty-one years on trawlers out of this port. Now I sit here and tell the gulls how it used to be. They've heard it. They stay for the chips.
Ned: Name's Ned. You look like someone who walks places. Bring me a haddock some day and I'll tell you a thing or two about the North Sea.
meet: Ned is leaning on a railing in Hull, watching the Humber go past with deep suspicion.
Ned: Funny. Everyone assumes a trawlerman knows every port. I've been to Hull four times and got lost on three of them.
Ned: Still. Good to see a face. Get yourself back to Whitby; I'm saving you the good bollard.
letter: I'm told you're meant to put your address at the top. I haven't got one, I've got a bollard. The gulls send their regards, and want it noted that they still don't like you.
offer: Ned: I'll say it plain, {player}. Your business wants someone to keep an eye on it while you're off walking. I've kept an eye on worse. A whole fleet, once. Most of it came back.
Ned: Give me the keys and a flask and I'll mind it.
chat: Ned: Tide's turning. It does that.
Ned: Never trust a gull that's been to college.
thanks: Ned takes the fish, sniffs it professionally and nods once.
Ned: That's a proper one. Nobody's brought me a proper one since 1998.

regulars.name: Gwenllian Pugh
regulars.hint: Gwenllian will do almost anything for a plate of Welsh cakes still warm from the bakestone.
intro: A woman with a tuning fork and the posture of a very small general is rehearsing nobody in particular.
Gwenllian: Gwenllian Pugh, choir mistress. Forty voices, three of them in tune on a good night. The altos are the problem. Don't tell the altos.
Gwenllian: You've the look of a baritone. No? Pity. Come back with Welsh cakes and I'll forgive you.
meet: Gwenllian is in Cardiff, standing in front of a statue, conducting it.
Gwenllian: Competition's tomorrow. We're going to lose to Pontypridd again and I'm going to be gracious about it through gritted teeth.
Gwenllian: You'll come and listen? Row C. Clap at the right bits. Row C knows when.
letter: We came second. Pontypridd came first. I was gracious. I have since broken a biro.
The altos hit the high note, which is a miracle I shall be citing at the next Eisteddfod. Come and hear us. Bring cakes.
offer: Gwenllian: Listen. Between rehearsals I've nothing to do but disapprove of people, and I'm running out of people.
Gwenllian: Let me run one of your businesses. I'll keep it tidy, on time and in four-part harmony.
chat: Gwenllian: Chin up. Shoulders back. Now sing.
Gwenllian: Nobody ever regretted learning a hymn.
thanks: Gwenllian: Welsh cakes! Still warm? Oh, you've been dear to me, {player}.
She eats three, with the tuning fork under her arm, and tells you it was for the altos.

regulars.name: Mervyn Hanna
regulars.hint: Mervyn lights up at a bowl of champ, spring onions and all.
intro: A big man in a flat cap is holding a tea flask like a tiller, gazing at the cranes by the water.
Mervyn: Forty-four years in the yard. Riveter, then foreman, then the man who knew where the tea was. Same thing, in the end.
Mervyn: Pull up a wall. I'll tell you how a hull goes together. Or champ, if you've any. I'd talk for a week for a bowl of champ.
meet: Mervyn is on the Liverpool waterfront, comparing the cranes to the ones at home. Home wins.
Mervyn: Visiting my sister. She's got opinions on my driving. I came on the ferry, so she's got opinions on that too.
Mervyn: Lovely city. Not enough Belfast in it, but nobody's perfect.
letter: Sister's put me out for putting milk in first. Back in Belfast now and the tea's right again.
The cranes say hello. They don't, but I do. Come by when you're passing.
offer: Mervyn: I managed forty men for forty years. One business is a doddle.
Mervyn: Show me the books and the kettle and I'll have it running like a launch day.
chat: Mervyn: Everything's built the same way. One plate at a time.
Mervyn: Never rush a weld. Never rush a pot of tea either.
thanks: Mervyn: Champ! With the butter well in the middle, the way it should be. You're a credit, {player}.
He eats it from the bowl, with a spoon, in total silence, which you understand is the highest praise.

regulars.name: Dessie Nolan
regulars.hint: Dessie will stop doing sums for a hot plate of Dublin coddle.
intro: A man in a waistcoat is working a pencil stub behind a counter with a very sincere face.
Dessie: Dessie Nolan. I take a small interest in horses and the horses take a large interest in me. Don't ask what the odds are on the weather. Depends who's asking.
Dessie: Sit down. I won't tell you a tip. I'll tell you a story, which is better, because it's free.
meet: Dessie is in Galway for the races, wearing the same waistcoat in a slightly different mood.
Dessie: Day three. I've lost on the grey, won on the bay, and I'm even. Even's a good place. Nobody gets robbed at even.
Dessie: Don't put a euro on anything you can't pat. That's my one rule. It's why I'm still here.
letter: Won a little, lost a little, a perfectly respectable week. I put a fiver on you getting the next Stone and you didn't let me down.
offer: Dessie: A man who can add can run anything. I can add. It's a quiet talent.
Dessie: Let me mind your business, {player}. I'll give it the same care I give a treble, which is a great deal, with a wee prayer.
chat: Dessie: The house always wins. I am the house. Don't tell me that's a conflict of interest.
Dessie: Never chase a loss. Walk to the chipper instead.
thanks: Dessie: Coddle! Sausage, bacon, potato, all in the one pot, like a family at Christmas. Good lad.
He eats it and recalculates three bets in his head, all in your favour, for the first time.

regulars.name: Morag MacLeod
regulars.hint: Morag has a soft spot for a slice of clootie dumpling.
intro: A woman at a loom the size of a small van is weaving something grey and enormous.
Morag: Morag. The tweed. You'll have heard of me, if you've heard of anyone. It takes me a month to make a coat and a week to forgive whoever buys it.
Morag: Sit. Mind the shuttle. You've good hands, I can tell, like a person who carries too much.
meet: Morag is in Inverness with a bale of wool, looking at the shops as if they were sheep.
Morag: They want me to make it thinner. Thinner! In this weather! I said it'll keep the rain out or it's a scarf.
Morag: Come north when the days are long. There's more light than you can use.
letter: The tweed is finished. It is, I'm told, 'a statement'. It is a coat. Someone in London paid a ridiculous amount and I've bought a new loom.
Come and see it. It weighs about the same as you. Morag
offer: Morag: I can weave for twelve hours and never lose a stitch. Counting takings is no different.
Morag: Hand me one of your businesses and I'll keep it in order, with a flask.
chat: Morag: Slow is a speed.
Morag: The wool tells you when it's ready. So does the weather.
thanks: Morag: A clootie dumpling! Spiced and boiled in a cloth the old way. You've the manners of a laird, {player}.
She cuts it in two even slices without looking, which seems to be the way she does everything.

regulars.name: Pauline Fogg
regulars.hint: Pauline will always make room for a bowl of Lancashire hotpot.
intro: A woman in a pinny and a flowered tabard is sweeping a doorstep that doesn't need sweeping.
Pauline: Pauline Fogg. Guesthouse, forty years, one star I haven't been told about. We've a vacancy and an opinion about everyone who's ever had one.
Pauline: Come in for a cuppa, love. Breakfast is eight till eight-oh-two. Don't be late, I'll know.
meet: Pauline is in Manchester at a conference on guesthouses. It's a very small conference.
Pauline: There was a talk on 'guest experience'. I've been giving guests an experience since before they had the word.
Pauline: Come and stay. There's a kettle in every room. Behave and you can have two.
letter: Had a lovely week. A man from Doncaster asked for a vegan sausage. I gave him a look. He had the bacon.
Come and see me. There's a room, and it's yours. Pauline xx
offer: Pauline: I've run a house of eleven rooms with one hand and a tea towel. I can run your business.
Pauline: I'll treat it like a guest, love. Fussed over and fed.
chat: Pauline: Never trust a man who puts ketchup on a full English before he's tasted it.
Pauline: Keep the kettle on. It solves everything except the roof.
thanks: Pauline: Hotpot! Proper lamb and sliced potatoes on top, all crispy! You're a darling, {player}.
She takes the bowl straight to the kitchen and comes back with a plate of her own, which she insists is 'just a taste'.

regulars.name: Barnaby Quill
regulars.hint: Barnaby's weakness is a good jar of Oxford marmalade.
intro: A thin old gentleman in a woolly hat is taking notes on a pigeon.
Barnaby: Barnaby Quill, retired verger. Ring bells on Thursdays. Sit on a bench on all the other days and take the town's pulse. Today it is slightly irregular.
Barnaby: Do you take your toast with marmalade? A man can judge you on that. I'll wait.
meet: Barnaby is on a bench in Cambridge, recording the punt traffic in a small, neat ledger.
Barnaby: Eleven punts in the first hour and only two sank. It's an improvement. In my day it was a bloodbath.
Barnaby: The bells in this town are very clean. I resent it, slightly.
letter: I got a rope burn from a Grandsire Triples touch and I'm rather pleased with it. It is the closest I've come to a wound.
offer: Barnaby: I keep a ledger of everything. A business is a bigger ledger with more shouting.
Barnaby: Give me yours to manage, {player}. I'll keep the sums as tidy as the bell frames.
chat: Barnaby: Patience is the only thing worth ringing.
Barnaby: The pigeon, I regret to say, is not what it seems.
thanks: Barnaby: Marmalade! Thick-cut, I trust? Oh, bless you. Bitter, orange and just slightly smug, like me.
He opens the jar, smells it and puts the lid back on with the air of a man saving something for later.

regulars.name: Fiona Gunn
regulars.hint: Fiona will stop a reel mid-bar for a bowl of Scotch broth.
intro: A woman with a fiddle under her chin is playing three tunes at once and hoping nobody counts them.
Fiona: Fiona. I play at every wedding on Skye and a few funerals, and the funerals pay better. It's the sandwiches.
Fiona: Sit. The next one's a reel and I'll need a witness.
meet: Fiona is in Glasgow, busking outside a pub that's pretending not to hear.
Fiona: Gallus lot, the Glaswegians. They tell you you're rubbish and then put a fiver in the case, which is a kind of love.
Fiona: Come up to the island in September. We've a ceilidh. Wear shoes you can lose.
letter: The ceilidh is September. The band is me, my cousin and a man called Archie who plays the spoons and does not take notes.
Bring a partner. Or don't. We'll find you one. Fiona
offer: Fiona: I can fiddle and count at the same time, which is more than most accountants.
Fiona: Let me look after one of your businesses and I'll play the staff a tune to keep their spirits up.
chat: Fiona: A reel is just a question. You answer it with your feet.
Fiona: Never tune in front of the bride.
thanks: Fiona: Scotch broth! Barley and neep and a bit of mutton. Perfect for the cold. Cheers, {player}.
She tucks a napkin in her collar, props the fiddle on her knee and eats like a woman who has played four hours straight.

regulars.name: Dot Armitage
regulars.hint: Dot is partial to a Cumberland sausage, the longer the better.
intro: A wiry woman in a bright anorak is stretching against a lamp post with the intensity of a cat.
Dot: Dot. Seventy-one. Fell runner, the old school. I ran Skiddaw every Sunday for fifty years and haven't worn a watch since the first. I know the time by my knees.
Dot: You walk a lot. Good. Don't stop. Once you stop the knees notice.
meet: Dot is in Carlisle, in a hurry, for no reason she's willing to explain.
Dot: Market day. I've got a list: sausages, a bag of sticky toffee and a pair of socks. In that order.
Dot: I did ten miles to get here. The bus was full. That's the Lake District for you.
letter: I went up Helvellyn with a sprained ankle. It turned out to be a very small sprain. I was wrong, and a bit embarrassed about it, but I got the view.
See you on the hill. Dot
offer: Dot: The thing about running fells is you can't see the finish. Running a business is the same, so I'd say I'm qualified.
Dot: Give it here, {player}. I'll run it up the hill and back before breakfast.
chat: Dot: If you can talk, you're not going fast enough.
Dot: Weather's a rumour until you're wet.
thanks: Dot: A proper Cumberland! Coiled like a snake and peppery enough to wake you. You're alright, {player}.
She eats it standing up, mid-stretch, without once breaking a sweat.

regulars.name: Seán Ó Súilleabháin
regulars.hint: Seán brightens up for a bowl of Irish stew.
intro: A man in a cap and a jumper nobody could unpick is coiling a rope on a quay with great tenderness.
Seán: Seán. I take people out to see the dolphin. Fungie's long gone but the tourists don't know yet and I'm not going to be the one to tell them.
Seán: You've a good face for the sea. Don't look at it like that, it's sensitive.
meet: Seán is in Cork for a funeral, a christening and a pint, in that order, and enjoying all three.
Seán: Everyone I've ever met is related to someone in Cork. It's a county-sized family and we're all very polite about it.
Seán: Come west when you can. I'll show you the sea. She loves company.
letter: I took the boat out in a swell the size of a small hill and came back with all my fingers. I count that a week well spent.
Come and visit. The tea's strong. Seán
offer: Seán: A boat teaches you to look after a place. Nobody sleeps till it's tied up.
Seán: Let me mind one of yours, {player}. I'll keep it afloat, and I'll sing at it.
chat: Seán: The sea doesn't do grudges. She does moods.
Seán: A kind word costs nothing, and it floats.
thanks: Seán: Irish stew! Mutton, spuds and onion, not a carrot in sight. A man of good taste, {player}.
He eats it with the gravity of a man at Mass, and wipes the bowl with bread.

regulars.name: Tamsin Penrose
regulars.hint: Tamsin always has a use for a fresh mackerel.
intro: A woman in a fisherman's smock is gutting a mackerel faster than you can follow.
Tamsin: Tamsin. I run the fish stall at the quay, and I've never lost a seagull fight. I've drawn a few.
Tamsin: A fish tells you everything if you look it in the eye. This one says it's very sorry.
meet: Tamsin is in Plymouth, looking over the Barbican with the confidence of someone selling you the harbour.
Tamsin: They sell fish here. Pah. Good fish, mind. But it's not my fish.
Tamsin: Come to Newlyn when the boats are in. It's the best theatre in Cornwall and the seats are free.
letter: The mackerel are running. It's a glorious thing. A thousand silver bodies, and every one of them is a lunch.
Come down when you can. I'll save you a bag. Tamsin
offer: Tamsin: Selling's my whole life. I can charm a stone out of a gull.
Tamsin: Let me work for you, {player}, and I'll have the takings up before you've had your tea.
chat: Tamsin: Never haggle with a woman holding a knife. Obvious really.
Tamsin: If it smells of fish, it's fresh. If it smells of nothing, run.
thanks: Tamsin: Mackerel! Fresh as a daisy and shining like a coin. You're a good sort, {player}.
She turns it over in her palm, approving, and tosses it into a bucket labelled 'for the cat, (me)'.

regulars.name: Hilda Pickles
regulars.hint: Hilda's fondness for a home-made Yorkshire pudding is well known.
intro: A neat woman in a headscarf is jotting down train numbers on a clipboard at the edge of a platform.
Hilda: Hilda Pickles. Thirty-eight years in the signal box, now retired, which means I do it unpaid. It's the same job with less shouting.
Hilda: Eleven forty-two to Leeds is late. It was late in 1987, too. Some things never change, and I'm told that's reassuring.
meet: Hilda is on a platform in Leeds, timing a train against her own wristwatch and tutting.
Hilda: Four seconds late. Four. In my day we'd have had a word with the driver. We'd have had a very quiet word.
Hilda: Don't look so worried, pet. The railway's grand. It's the people on it.
letter: The 11.42 was on time yesterday. I wrote to the company to say so. They have not replied. I assume they're sending flowers.
offer: Hilda: I ran a whole junction on a lever and a prayer. A bit of tea-shop bookkeeping is nothing.
Hilda: Hand it over, {player}. It'll run to the timetable. My timetable.
chat: Hilda: A minute late is a minute stolen.
Hilda: Always close the door. You don't know who's behind it.
thanks: Hilda: Yorkshire pudding! Home-made and risen like a church steeple. Well done, {player}. You'd make a good signalwoman.
She eats it with gravy from a flask she was, you realise, already carrying.

regulars.name: Old Tom
regulars.hint: Old Tom says a tench from the Kennet and Avon is the only thing worth eating after a cold night at the eyepiece.
intro: Old Tom: Not many people stop to ask what I'm looking at. It's the Moon. It's always the Moon. I'm very fond of it.
Old Tom: Tom, if you like. Everyone adds the Old. Bring me a tench from the canal some day and I'll let you have a go on the eyepiece.
meet: Old Tom is on the Bristol waterfront with the telescope in a pram, pointing it at a gull.
Old Tom: It's a test. The gull is a very bad planet. Good to see you, though. Come home to Bath, the kettle's on and the sky's clearing.
letter: Clear skies here for once. Caroline Herschel would have been out all night; I managed forty minutes and a biscuit. The Moon sends its regards.
offer: Old Tom: Now then, {player}. That business of yours. It wants someone to mind the shop while you're off looking at the sky, or whatever it is you do.
Old Tom: I've sat up all night with a telescope. A till won't frighten me.
chat: Old Tom: Mars is up. Reddish. Sulking, I think.
Old Tom: Don't breathe on the lens. Herschel would have said so, and he was a polite man.
thanks: Old Tom turns the tench over like a rare comet.
Old Tom: Well, that's a find. I'll name it. Gerald.

regulars.name: Maureen Armstrong
regulars.hint: Mrs Armstrong says a proper Cumberland sausage, coiled and peppery, is the only thing she would ever accept from a visitor.
intro: Mrs Armstrong: Now we're settled, I'll say it. Everyone expects a clan of reivers and gets a woman with a tea towel. Disappointing for them, restful for me.
Mrs Armstrong: Maureen, to my friends. Bring me a proper Cumberland sausage, the coiled sort, and I'll count you as one. Cousins get two.
meet: Mrs Armstrong is outside a Newcastle department store, guarding a carrier bag from nobody in particular.
Mrs Armstrong: My sister married a Geordie. We don't discuss it. I counted the spoons on the way out, purely from habit.
Mrs Armstrong: Don't look like that, pet. I put them back.
letter: The cat has stolen a sock and hidden it behind the settle. I have said nothing, on the grounds that it takes after the family. Nobody has been hanged this week, so I call it a success.
offer: Mrs Armstrong: Your business wants minding while you're off tramping about. I've kept a house full of Armstrongs in order, and that's harder than any till.
Mrs Armstrong: Leave it with me. I'll count the takings twice. That's called being careful, pet, whatever the neighbours say.
chat: Mrs Armstrong: Don't mind the cat. It has never hurt anyone who wasn't carrying fish.
Mrs Armstrong: An Armstrong never forgets a favour, or a slight. Luckily I'm not holding any against you.
Mrs Armstrong: Border weather is just the Debatable Land arguing with itself.
thanks: Mrs Armstrong weighs the sausage in her hand, then sniffs it like a customs officer.
Mrs Armstrong: Cumberland, and not a crumb of a lie in it. You're welcome in this house any day, pet. Mind the cat.

regulars.name: Walter Gibson
regulars.hint: Farmer Walt says an Arctic charr out of the deep water is the one fish he would stop work for.
intro: Farmer Walt: Walt. Walter if I'm in trouble.
Farmer Walt: Herdwicks, forty acres and a dog that doesn't listen. That's the lot. Bring me a charr from the lake some day. I'd be glad of it.
meet: Farmer Walt is leaning on a pen at Carlisle mart, saying nothing to a great many sheep.
Farmer Walt: Selling tups. Or watching them not sell. Same day's work, really.
Farmer Walt: Folk talk too much at these things. I've said eleven words since dinner. All of them were 'no'.
letter: Lambs are fine. Dog is not. It is exactly as it was. The kettle has been on all week, as per law.
Yours, Walt (Gibson, no relation to the dog)
offer: Farmer Walt: You've a business that wants minding. I mind sheep. They're worse than customers.
Farmer Walt: I'll do it. Shan't talk much, mind.
chat: Farmer Walt: Rain's coming. Can tell by the dog. It's gone under the table.
Farmer Walt: Kettle's on.
Farmer Walt: Beatrix Potter had a good eye for a Herdwick. Better than mine, and I've had mine on them sixty years.
thanks: Farmer Walt turns the charr over, grunts, and for once does not say no.
Farmer Walt: Well. That's a fish. Sit down, I'll put the kettle on. It's on. Sit down anyway.

regulars.name: Harold Procter
regulars.hint: Mr Procter says a perch off the towpath, striped and cheerful, is what a retired boatman really wants for his tea.
intro: Mr Procter: Harold, I should say. Forty years on the cut, and I still look for a mooring when I sit down, and then I remember I live in a house.
Mr Procter: I'd say come back with a perch, bring a perch, any perch off the towpath, and we'll have it fried, with butter, and I'll tell you about the time I lost a whole barge. Briefly.
meet: Mr Procter is in Llangollen, leaning on a rail above the canal and looking at the boats with one raised eyebrow.
Mr Procter: Very narrow, this one. And that aqueduct. Right up in the air. I went across it holding my breath, and not out of fear, mind, just respect.
Mr Procter: Forty miles with no locks at home, and here's a canal that has all of them. Lovely, though. Lovely. I got lost looking for the lock.
letter: I have been sat in the window all week saying 'aboard' to the postman, and he has finally started to answer 'aye aye'. I think it is a form of progress, though it may be a form of pity. Anyway the canal is restful.
Yours, Harold (Procter, Captain, retired, of the front room)
offer: Mr Procter: Now, {player}, I've been thinking. A business is like a boat. It needs a steady hand and a very long cup of tea.
Mr Procter: Let me mind it. I won't rock it. Forty years and never once rocked it, except the one time, which was a swan.
chat: Mr Procter: Restful, a canal. The only thing that rushes on it is the ducks, and they're only pretending.
Mr Procter: I said 'port' to the milkman. He said 'what'. So I said 'left' and he understood. I miss the old days.
Mr Procter: Zigzlets? Still lost, I'd say. Same as me when someone moves the furniture.
thanks: Mr Procter holds up the perch to the light like a man checking a gauge.
Mr Procter: Splendid. Stripes and all. Now I shall be a bore for the rest of the evening, and you are welcome to stay and enjoy it.

regulars.name: Eddie Kenny
regulars.hint: Eddie says a pot of Dublin coddle is what half of Liverpool grew up on, and the other half wishes it had.
intro: Eddie: Eddie. Warden. I wardens things. Mostly pillars. They've not complained.
Eddie: My nan came over from Dublin on the boat. She said you've not lived till you've had a coddle on a wet Tuesday. Bring me one and I'll agree with her.
meet: Eddie is on the ferry terminal at Douglas, looking at a pillar and seeming a little betrayed by it.
Eddie: Day trip. This one's stone. Not even iron. I was told it was sturdy. I'm not convinced.
Eddie: Don't tell the Albert Dock. It'd take it personally.
letter: Nothing has fallen on anyone this week. I put that in the logbook, and the logbook has never looked so thin. The pillars send their regards, in that they have not moved.
Yours, Eddie (Kenny, Warden of the Pillars, unofficially)
offer: Eddie: Look, {player}. I stand in a building all day and make sure it doesn't fall. A shop's easier. It has a till.
Eddie: Give it here. I'll keep an eye on the roof and the stock. In that order.
chat: Eddie: Cast iron. Not a stick of wood. Very sensible. I've nothing to add. I've said it about four thousand times.
Eddie: A man once asked me if the pillars were load-bearing. I said they were bearing it very well.
Eddie: Victorians built it to last. I'm here to make sure they're right.
thanks: Eddie lifts the lid, breathes in, and nods slowly, like a man who has just been reunited with his nan.
Eddie: Coddle. Right. That'll do. You're all right, you. I'd say more, but I'd only get misty.

regulars.name: Alf Dutton
regulars.hint: Old Alf says a sea bass, silver and sulky, is the only thing the Dee ever gave him that he'd call a fair swap.
intro: Old Alf: Alf. Old Alf, if you're being kind. This used to be a harbour. Now it's a view. I'm in the view.
Old Alf: Bring me a sea bass some day. Proper one, off the shore. I'll let you sit in the boat. It doesn't go anywhere, but it's the thought.
meet: Old Alf is on the quay at Holyhead, watching the Irish ferry as though it has overtaken his career.
Old Alf: The packet boats left Parkgate when the water went. They came here. Cheeky. Nobody asked me.
Old Alf: Mind you, this lot still has water. Proper water. I'm not bitter. I've just been standing here a while.
letter: The tide came in on Thursday and I had a little cry. Not really. But the marsh looked grand, and the birds seemed pleased, and I thought of the ships. Then I had a sandwich.
Yours, Alf (Dutton, Harbourmaster of the Marsh)
offer: Old Alf: A business is only a boat that stays put. I know boats that stay put. I'm in one.
Old Alf: Give me the keys, {player}. I'll sit in your shop and watch it like a tide. It'll come in, I'm told.
chat: Old Alf: Handel landed right here. Said nothing about the weather. Very polite.
Old Alf: The water went and the birds came. Better company, if you ask me. They don't talk back.
Old Alf: Tide's out. It's been out since 1800 or so. It might come back.
thanks: Old Alf holds the bass up and looks it in the eye, like an old rival.
Old Alf: Well now. That's silver, that is. You've done me proud, {player}. I'll sit in the boat and think about it.

regulars.name: Doreen Marsh
regulars.hint: Doreen says a Yorkshire pudding that has risen properly is the one thing she would swap a Sunday for.
intro: Doreen: Doreen. Sit, sit. My grandson's keeping goal in the garden and the washing is losing. I don't mind, I'd rather watch that than the telly.
Doreen: Do you cook? A Yorkshire pudding, home-made, risen high. That's all I want in this world, apart from a clean sheet for our Callum.
meet: Doreen is in Manchester at a goalkeeping trial, with a flask and the face of a woman who has opinions.
Doreen: He let in six. I've told him it's the posts' fault. He's not buying it. Kids don't, these days.
Doreen: Sheffield FC, oldest in the world, and nobody here's even heard of it. I told the ref. He said 'who?'
letter: Callum saved a penalty on Saturday. He leapt about eight feet, and landed on the washing, which was on the line, which still had my best tablecloth on it. I have never been prouder, or lost so many pegs.
offer: Doreen: You've a business, haven't you, love. Who's minding it while you're off? I'll do it.
Doreen: I've run a household of five on a Sunday. A till won't frighten me, and I'll keep it cleaner than the washing.
chat: Doreen: The washing line's been a goal, a trampoline and a battleground. It's held up better than my knees.
Doreen: Sit down, sit down. You can't stand there like a vicar.
Doreen: Callum wants to play for England. I told him to start with the garden.
thanks: Doreen peels back the foil, looks at the height of it and says nothing for a moment.
Doreen: It's risen. It's actually risen. Well done, love. Sit down, sit down. I'll get the gravy, and you can tell me everything.

regulars.name: Emeka Okafor
regulars.hint: Mr Okafor says a roach from the cut is a small, honest fish, and he has fished for them since the buses stopped.
intro: Mr Okafor: Okafor. Emeka, on weekends. Thirty years on the Number 11, and I still signal at the kettle.
Mr Okafor: I fish the cut now. A roach is all I ask. Small, silver, no nonsense. Bring me one and I'll tell you the exact time every bus ought to have arrived.
meet: Mr Okafor is on a coach outside Blackpool Tower, checking his watch against a timetable nobody gave him.
Mr Okafor: My wife's birthday. She wanted lights. I wanted a seat. We both got what we wanted, except the seat was her handbag.
Mr Okafor: A tram in front of the Tower is on time, I see. I'm impressed. I'm also annoyed.
letter: I caught nothing on Saturday, which is no worse than the 11 did to its timetable. The heron watched me the whole time, and I think it was judging. My wife says it was admiring.
offer: Mr Okafor: A business is a route, {player}. Same stops, same people, and a delay if you're not careful.
Mr Okafor: I'll drive it for you. Thirty years, no accidents. Well. One. It was a pigeon.
chat: Mr Okafor: Mom, bus, dinner. Say it right. Whole mouth.
Mr Okafor: I still brake at corners. The wife has stopped complaining. She has started a tally.
Mr Okafor: A strutcoo outside my window has a view on the council. It's about as useful as the council.
thanks: Mr Okafor takes the roach, looks it over for a good ten seconds, then nods like a man signing off a service.
Mr Okafor: On time and in good order. That's a good fish. Right, sit down. I'll tell you about the Number 11. It will not take long. It will.

regulars.name: Cuthbert Haines
regulars.hint: Mr Haines says a mutton stew, onion and potato and nothing fancy, is what a wool man eats to remember the flock.
intro: Mr Haines: Haines. Cuthbert, but nobody uses it. I grade wool, which is to say I rub it between my fingers and look disappointed. I am very good at it.
Mr Haines: A hot mutton stew would be most acceptable, if you were passing. Irish, they call it, though a sheep does not care where it is from.
meet: Mr Haines is at a London wool warehouse, rubbing a swatch between finger and thumb and shaking his head at the ceiling.
Mr Haines: A merchant told me it was 'a very good fleece'. It was fine. Medium. Not a hint of lustre. I told him so, very gently, with a mallet.
Mr Haines: Not really a mallet. A look. It has the same effect.
letter: A bale came in this week which I would have called a masterpiece, had it not been put in the wrong shed. I have since said so to the shed. There is a lesson in it, and I intend to find it.
Yours, Cuthbert Haines (Stapler, Grader of Fleeces, Fusser)
offer: Mr Haines: A business is a bale, {player}. One needs to know the length of the fibre, and the price, and which of the two is lying.
Mr Haines: Let me manage yours. I shall be thorough, and slightly smug.
chat: Mr Haines: A Cotswold sheep once had customers in Florence. I have had customers in Stroud, and it is not the same.
Mr Haines: Length, lustre, weight. That is all one needs to know about wool. And people.
Mr Haines: Never judge a fleece by its mud. Judge it afterwards, and be ready to be wrong.
thanks: Mr Haines lifts the lid, inhales slowly and closes his eyes, as though grading it.
Mr Haines: Long, rich and heavy. The finest I have met in a pot. You have a good hand, {player}. I shall tell no one. Or everyone.

regulars.name: Hetty Boycott
regulars.hint: Hetty says a bowl of cawl is the only toll she will accept from a friend.
intro: Hetty: Hetty Boycott, Toll Keeper. I've no tolls to collect now, but I sit here with the little window open, in case old habits want a visit.
Hetty: Everyone pays something to cross, in the end. I'd take a bowl of cawl. Lamb, leek, nothing fussy. Call it the usual rate.
meet: Hetty is in Shrewsbury, holding the door of a shop and asking each person who goes in for a penny. Several have paid.
Hetty: Habit. I give it back at the end. Mostly. Most of them don't even notice.
Hetty: Better than being asked for fifteen pounds to park.
letter: Nobody has crossed the bridge without saying 'ooh' this week, and I've counted. It's a hundred and four ooohs, and four of them were genuine. I put the rest in the book under 'courtesy'.
Yours, Hetty (Boycott, Tolls, Retired, Still Counting)
offer: Hetty: A business is only a bridge with a till at one end. I know both ends.
Hetty: Let me mind yours, {player}. Nobody's ever got past me without paying, and nobody's ever minded.
chat: Hetty: Pay up or ooh. Those are the two choices.
Hetty: It's iron, that bridge. It's held up better than I have, and it's older.
Hetty: A penny to cross. A smile to stay. That's the toll.
thanks: Hetty takes the bowl in both hands and breathes it in, as though paying herself a small compliment.
Hetty: Cawl. You've paid in full, {player}, with interest. I'll put you down as a regular. I mean it. Sit.

regulars.name: Hugh Fenwick
regulars.hint: Hugh says a good eel from the Witham, stewed the old way, is the most honest medieval dish still going.
intro: Hugh: Hugh Fenwick. I look after this house, or it looks after me. We've not agreed on which. Stone since about 1160. I find it very patient.
Hugh: I'd be glad of an eel from the Witham some time. Stewed, not jellied. A man can only take so much history on an empty stomach.
meet: Hugh is in York, standing in front of a wall and apologising to it, for reasons he declines to explain.
Hugh: I'm here for a conference. Four hundred historians, one urn of tea. It is turning into a chapter of its own.
Hugh: I asked a man where the thirteenth century was. He said 'down the Shambles'. It may even be true.
letter: I have been in the archive all week and have discovered that a lot of people died, and several of them owed money. I find this oddly comforting. The house sends its regards, in the form of a draught.
Yours, Hugh (Fenwick, of the Stone House, in spirit)
offer: Hugh: A business is a very small archive that sells things. I can keep records. It's the selling I'd need to work on.
Hugh: Let me manage yours. I'll be accurate, if slow, and I'll footnote the till.
chat: Hugh: The house remembers. I merely write it down. It's a good arrangement. It doesn't argue.
Hugh: Aaron of Lincoln lent to kings and abbeys. I lend people a chair. We each do what we can.
Hugh: Stone lasts. People, rather less. I try to remember both.
thanks: Hugh unwraps the eel carefully and sets it on the table like an exhibit.
Hugh: A fine specimen. Medieval cooks would have wept. Thank you, {player}. I'll make notes, and then I'll eat it.

regulars.name: Mavis Hallam
regulars.hint: Nanna Mavis says a Bakewell pudding, jam and almond, is what you bring to a Nottingham nan if you want to be asked back.
intro: Nanna Mavis: Ay up, me duck. Mavis. Nanna Mavis to anyone under sixty and to a good few over. I've a mardy grandson and a clean jitty, and I keep both in order.
Nanna Mavis: Bring me a Bakewell pudding. Jam on the bottom, almond on top. That's all. Next door's is a tart and I won't hear otherwise.
meet: Nanna Mavis is in Lincoln at the Christmas market, in a bobble hat, buying everything on a stall and explaining it to the stallholder.
Nanna Mavis: Up the hill, down the hill, up the hill. They've no jitties here, just hills. I said it to a bloke and he said 'it's Lincoln'. Cheeky.
Nanna Mavis: Gizza cob? I said it to the baker. He gave me a roll and a look. Don't say please, I said. It spoils the effect.
letter: Our Kyle has been mardy since Tuesday and I've told him it'll wear off like a bad perm. I met the lions at the Council House on Saturday, and they didn't say owt, which I thought was rude.
Yours, Nanna Mavis (Hallam, of the jitty)
offer: Nanna Mavis: You've a business, me duck. Who's minding it while you're gadding about? I will.
Nanna Mavis: I've kept a house of four generations in line with a wooden spoon. A till is easy, and it doesn't answer back.
chat: Nanna Mavis: Kettle's on, me duck. It's always on. Don't make me say it again.
Nanna Mavis: Left Lion, ten o'clock. Don't be late, and don't be mardy.
Nanna Mavis: A cob is a bread roll. I've said so to the vicar. He's not a cob person. Pity.
thanks: Nanna Mavis lifts the lid, sniffs the almond and takes a very small, very proud step backwards.
Nanna Mavis: Bakewell pudding! Jam and all. You're a good 'un, me duck. Sit down. There's tea, and I've not finished telling you about the jitty.

regulars.name: Wilf Ashby
regulars.hint: Wilf says a roach from the Cam would be the best thing to happen to a long week of problem sets.
intro: Wilf: Sorry, I was proving something. It turned out to be proved already, in 1750. I find that happens rather a lot.
Wilf: Wilf, by the way. Bring me a roach from the Cam some day. I fish between problem sets, and so far the roach are winning.
meet: Wilf is on a street in Lincoln, holding a bag of washing and a train timetable as though both were unsolved problems.
Wilf: Home for the weekend. Newton came home to Lincolnshire to think. I came home to get my socks done.
Wilf: Same result, in fairness. Fewer apples.
letter: Cambridge is quiet and the beetles are safe. I keep one hand free at all times, in case. Darwin would approve, or at least he would not bite. Last week's proof still only works on Tuesdays.
offer: Wilf: I could mind your business while you walk, {player}. It is mostly stock, queues and margins. I have a supervision on queues.
Wilf: I would be quite sensible about it. I count things for fun. Ask my landlady.
chat: Wilf: Newton had a plague. I have a deadline. I got the better deal, though not by much.
Wilf: Turing was at King's. I walk past it daily and feel suitably small.
Wilf: A good proof is like a good punt. It looks effortless and someone is quietly getting wet.
thanks: Wilf lifts the roach by the tail and measures it against his thumb, then his forearm, then his thumb again.
Wilf: Excellent. Twelve centimetres, give or take, and nothing about it is irrational. Thank you, {player}.

regulars.name: Marion Pettit
regulars.hint: Marion says a fresh plaice from the Channel is her Friday treat after a week of schoolchildren.
intro: Marion: Right, the quick version. Roman hotel, painted walls, heating under the floor, fort on top. Questions at the end. There are always questions about the toilets.
Marion: Marion, I do the tours. Bring me a plaice off the Dover shore and I will show you the best bit of wall. Nobody gets that.
meet: Marion is in Canterbury with a clipboard, counting a coach party of Year Sevens in front of the cathedral.
Marion: Hands in pockets, nobody lick the cathedral. Oh, hello. I have been on my feet since seven.
Marion: Dover is easier. The walls stay where you put them. Well, where the Romans did.
letter: Nobody has fallen off the walkway this term, a small victory. The Romans buried the lower walls by accident and I tell the children it was good planning. Nobody checks.
offer: Marion: I take forty children round a Roman hotel and have never lost one. A shop is a gentle morning.
Marion: Give me the keys, {player}. Queue to the left, questions at the end.
chat: Marion: Heating under the floor, eighteen hundred years ago. My flat has a radiator that knocks.
Marion: Red, yellow and green. They knew what they were doing with a paintbrush.
Marion: Everything in Dover is buried under something else. I find it restful.
thanks: Marion holds the plaice up to the light as if it might be painted on a wall.
Marion: Perfect. Flat, honest and from the Channel. Thank you, {player}. Now mind the step, there is always a step.

regulars.name: Dolly Vowles
regulars.hint: Granny Vowles says a Levels eel, fried with a bit of bacon, is what her own granny put on the table.
intro: Granny Vowles: Sit down, my lover, you are making the cat nervous. Dolly, if you must, but the postman calls me Granny and he is not even family.
Granny Vowles: I would be glad of an eel off the Levels, if you come by one. Fried with bacon. The cat can have the head.
meet: Granny Vowles is on a bench in Bristol, handbag on her knee, watching a gull steal a chip.
Granny Vowles: My granddaughter lives up here, my lover. All this traffic. She says the same about my cat.
Granny Vowles: Ansum to see you. That is lovely, in case you had forgotten.
letter: The Holy Thorn is in bud early, so the children think Christmas is coming. I let them. The hazeldoze are still asleep and I am still jealous. The cat sends no regards. He never does.
Yours, Granny Vowles (and the cat, under protest)
offer: Granny Vowles: I raised four children and one very rude cat, my lover. A till will not frighten me.
Granny Vowles: Off you go walking. I will give short change a look, and no change at all.
chat: Granny Vowles: The cat sat on the Thorn sprig again. I think he believes it is his.
Granny Vowles: A gurt big plate of anything, that is what a body wants. Mr Pomeroy taught me that.
Granny Vowles: Half a year asleep would suit me. I would have to feed the cat first.
thanks: Granny Vowles takes the eel in a tea towel like a baby, and tells it it has had a very long journey.
Granny Vowles: Oh, that is a proper one. Ansum, my lover, ansum. Stay for supper, I insist.

regulars.name: Alf Rudge
regulars.hint: Alf says a Thames chub fights harder than any student on the pole and he is not sure why he likes it so much.
intro: Alf: Alf. Punts by the hour. Sloping end, remember. Stand where you like, I have seen worse.
Alf: I would be glad of a chub, if you chance on one. All fight and very little taste. I have never understood why I like them.
meet: Alf is on the Backs in Cambridge, arms folded, watching a punt go by with the punter standing on the till.
Alf: Wrong end. Entirely the wrong end. And they say we are the odd ones.
Alf: I am here for the day. Industrial espionage. Do not tell anyone, I am very bad at it.
letter: Business is steady. There was a splash at Magdalen Bridge on Tuesday. I did not look. It was not me. Possibly. The hat has not been recovered. The pole, I am glad to say, was.
offer: Alf: Running a business is like punting. Keep hold of the pole, pull it out smartly, and do not look when there is a splash.
Alf: I will mind yours, {player}. Standing at the right end.
chat: Alf: Cambridge stand on the till. Poor souls. They cannot help it.
Alf: Rule one is keep hold of the pole. Most people forget rule one and then the others do not matter.
Alf: Quiet day. Only two in the river, and one of them meant it.
thanks: Alf lays the chub across his knee and regards it with the slow respect of a man looking at an old rival.
Alf: Ugly beast. Marvellous. Thank you, {player}. You can have the good pole next time.

regulars.name: Dougie Tucker
regulars.hint: Dougie says a sardine on toast from the Barbican beats any half-time pie at Home Park.
intro: Dougie: Dougie. Kit man. I wash the green shirts, I find the missing socks, and once I found a goalkeeper. Proper job, that.
Dougie: Bring me a sardine off the quay, my lover, and I will grill it on toast. Better than any pre-match talk in the tunnel.
meet: Dougie is outside St James Park in Exeter, carrying a kit bag the size of a small dog and glaring at the sky.
Dougie: Devon derby. Same county, same weather, worse parking. We always win in my head.
Dougie: Do not tell the lads I am nervous. I am only nervous about the shirts.
letter: The pitch is lovely. I rolled it twice, then once more for luck, then stood on the touchline and told it to behave. Do not walk on it. You will be tempted. We all are. The green army marches on.
offer: Dougie: I fold forty shirts every Friday and not one has ever gone missing. Your business will be fine.
Dougie: Off you go, {player}. I will keep it tidy. I will even roll the doormat, in case.
chat: Dougie: Argyle since 1886. Some seasons it has felt like every one of those years.
Dougie: Rain coming. I can feel it in the boots.
Dougie: Nobody knows where Argyle comes from. I just wash the shirts.
thanks: Dougie sets the sardine on a slice of toast so quickly you suspect he had planned it.
Dougie: Proper job, {player}. Salt, smoke and butter. Match day starts here.

regulars.name: Nesta Hafren
regulars.hint: Mrs Hafren says a warm Welsh cake is the one thing that stops her son talking about the bore for ten whole minutes.
intro: Mrs Hafren: Nesta, if you like, though the whole bridge calls me Mrs Hafren. Come in, mind the telescope, it points at the mud for the birds.
Mrs Hafren: I would be glad of a Welsh cake, a warm one. My son stops talking about the bore while he eats. It is the only quiet we get.
meet: Mrs Hafren is outside a shop window in Cardiff, holding a child's lifejacket at arm's length as though it might go off.
Mrs Hafren: He wants a board. I told him a bath comes first. He says he has had a bath. I said a long one.
Mrs Hafren: Lovely to see you, though. Welsh air and no bridge in sight. I can almost breathe.
letter: The Murmurants came over the mud at dusk again, a thousand of them with one idea. My son watched them all week and has not mentioned the bore once. I am afraid to say anything in case it starts him off.
offer: Mrs Hafren: I have watched a bridge and a boy for years. A little business will be a rest.
Mrs Hafren: Leave it with me, {player}. If the tide comes in I will simply move the stock.
chat: Mrs Hafren: The wind off the estuary rattles every window. I call it conversation.
Mrs Hafren: My son says he will ride the bore after tea. He says it every day. Tea has not yet finished.
Mrs Hafren: At low tide the mud goes on for miles. Do not walk on it. I say this to everyone.
thanks: Mrs Hafren holds the Welsh cake to her nose, still warm from the bakestone, and closes her eyes for a moment.
Mrs Hafren: Diolch, {player}. That is thank you, in case you wondered. The bridge will survive another week.

regulars.name: Ellen Quayle
regulars.hint: Mrs Quayle says a fresh herring takes her back to Peel kippers and her mother's kitchen.
intro: Mrs Quayle: Moghrey mie. Ellen, but Mrs Quayle will do, the whole street says so. Traa dy liooar, there is no hurry, sit.
Mrs Quayle: I would be glad of a herring if you pass the harbour. Kippers the Peel way, that is smoke and patience.
meet: Mrs Quayle is on the Pier Head in Liverpool with a suitcase, counting the seagulls out loud.
Mrs Quayle: Over on the boat to see my sister. I said traa dy liooar to the ticket man and he did not laugh.
Mrs Quayle: My grandson is counting horns on the gulls. Gulls do not have horns. He is counting anyway.
letter: My grandson has counted the horns on every loaghtan in the field and arrived at a number I cannot repeat in company. He sleeps well, though. The language class goes on. Traa dy liooar, as ever.
offer: Mrs Quayle: I raised a family and a Manx grandson. A shop on the quay is a morning's work, and I have the afternoon, traa dy liooar.
Mrs Quayle: Go on, {player}. I will keep the books and the rest can wait.
chat: Mrs Quayle: Fastyr mie, that is good afternoon. Practise it, the girl at the school says it is easy.
Mrs Quayle: Ned Maddrell would be pleased, you know. A whole school learning the old tongue.
Mrs Quayle: A loaghtan wants to be left alone. So do I, mostly, but with biscuits.
thanks: Mrs Quayle turns the herring in the light, silver as a coin, and nods like a woman receiving a long-lost relative.
Mrs Quayle: Gura mie ayd, {player}. That is thank you. Put the kettle on, I will do the rest.

regulars.name: Dave Warren
regulars.hint: Old Dave says a wahoo fresh off the line is the finest thing a longboat can bring home.
intro: Old Dave: Dave. Cox of the longboat for longer than the boat has had paint. Sit, you have the look of someone who has never rowed through surf.
Old Dave: I would be glad of a wahoo, caught properly. Fried plain with a bit of salt, and not a word spoken until it is finished.
meet: Old Dave is on a London street, standing very still and looking at a puddle as though he might have to row it.
Old Dave: Came for a family thing. Millions of people and not one of them can tell me where the sea is. I keep checking.
Old Dave: Do not tell them I have been aiming for the gap in the pavement. It is habit.
letter: The longboat went out twice this week and came back both times. Fifty years on and the sea still surprises me. I aimed for the gap, I prayed and I rowed. Two out of three, as ever.
offer: Old Dave: I take a boat through surf with six oars and a prayer. A business on dry land holds no fear for me.
Old Dave: Leave it with me, {player}. I will aim for the gap in the queue.
chat: Old Dave: Sea is in a mood. It is always in a mood. You learn to be glad it is a mood and not a plan.
Old Dave: Fifty years on the boats and the only thing that has changed is the knees.
Old Dave: Two out of three is a fine day. I would take it over a perfect one, I would have to row twice.
thanks: Old Dave lifts the wahoo, long and steel-blue, and weighs it in his hands like an old oar.
Old Dave: Now that is a fish. Thank you, {player}. Come by the boathouse and I will tell you about the one that got away.

regulars.name: Cecil Darrell
regulars.hint: Cecil says a yellowtail snapper, grilled plain, is the only thing that makes the steps worth climbing.
intro: Cecil: Cecil Darrell. Keeper. Welcome to the hundred and eighty-odd steps. I say odd because I have counted, and it is odd every time. The number, I mean. Possibly the steps too.
Cecil: If you come by a yellowtail snapper I would be glad of one. A man gets hungry at about step forty and there is no snack bar. I have suggested one.
meet: Cecil is on the waterfront in Boston, one hand shading his eyes, looking up at a very tall building and counting.
Cecil: Over to see my cousin. The hotel lift has a button for every floor and no steps at all. I took the stairs out of loyalty.
Cecil: Different number again, mind. It always is.
letter: The light is burning well and the weather has been kind. A dark wall came in over the sea on Tuesday and I did as always. Kettle, then supper. I counted the steps and got a number. I am keeping it quiet in case it holds.
offer: Cecil: I have kept a light burning for years. A shop that opens at nine is nothing to a man who stays up for ships.
Cecil: Leave it to me, {player}. I will even count the till twice. Differently, probably.
chat: Cecil: The visitor has still not recovered. I told him the view is lovely. He will take my word for it.
Cecil: When the sky goes dark over the sea, put the kettle on. That is the whole of my weather forecasting.
Cecil: A hundred and ten metres up. On a good day you can see all the way to slightly dizzy.
thanks: Cecil lifts the snapper, bright yellow along the flank, and nods slowly as if counting it.
Cecil: One. Lovely. Thank you, {player}. I may even get the same count twice.

regulars.name: Rita Summers
regulars.hint: Rita says a fresh sea trout from the river would earn the biggest smile at the smoko table.
intro: Rita: Rita. Sit, kettle is on. If you have come for smoko you will have a scone, and if you have come to talk you will have two.
Rita: A sea trout would be gladly received, if you have a rod and the patience. The men go quiet for a sea trout. It is the only time they do.
meet: Rita is in Stanley outside a shop, balancing four bags of shopping, a box of scones and a tin of paint.
Rita: Flew in for the shops. A week's worth in a morning, and the paint is for the roof. Do not ask.
Rita: The stove is in good hands. I told it to behave. It never goes out and I would rather not test it.
letter: The stove is still lit, thank goodness. I keep an eye on it the way other people keep an eye on the neighbours. The diddle-dee jam went well this year. Smoko is at eleven and four and I mean to keep it so.
offer: Rita: I feed six hungry men twice a day and keep a house warm in a gale. A business is easy. I will have it tidy by smoko.
Rita: Off you go, {player}. The kettle goes on first. That is how it begins.
chat: Rita: Peat and a tin roof, and the wind outside trying its best. I would not swap it.
Rita: Diddle-dee jam on a warm scone. If that is not worth a gale, I do not know what is.
Rita: The men will eat anything with mince in. I have tested this. Repeatedly.
thanks: Rita takes the sea trout in both hands and looks at it the way the men look at the weather.
Rita: Lovely, {player}. That will go on the table at four. Smoko, mind. Stay if you like.

regulars.name: Joyce Yon
regulars.hint: Joyce says a fresh yellowfin tuna is the pride of any Saint's table and she is particular about the freshness.
intro: Joyce: Joyce Yon. I look after the Governor's diary, the Governor's guests and, increasingly, the Governor's tortoise. Welcome.
Joyce: A yellowfin tuna would be warmly received. We Saints eat a good deal of it, and we are rather particular about the freshness.
meet: Joyce is in Georgetown on Ascension with a clipboard, a stack of folders and the look of someone who would like her tea.
Joyce: Island business. St Helena and Ascension have much to say to each other, mostly by post. This meeting began at ten and ended, in spirit, at ten past.
Joyce: Do sit. The tortoise is not here, so you may relax.
letter: The Governor is well, the lawn is perfect and Jonathan has taken to sleeping in the shade by the office door, which has given a few guests a surprise. Sir Hudson Lowe is still not loved, I am pleased to say.
offer: Joyce: I schedule a Governor. A business will not trouble me.
Joyce: I will have the diary, the till and the lawn in order, {player}. The tortoise has right of way, as ever.
chat: Joyce: This house has had many lodgers. Few were as quiet as Jonathan.
Joyce: Sir Hudson Lowe lived here. If the walls could talk, I would ask them to be polite.
Joyce: On the hot afternoons the tortoise comes in. I do not ask why. I suspect the shade is better than it looks.
thanks: Joyce takes the tuna, glances at it with the eye of someone who has judged many a plate, and nods.
Joyce: A Saint's fish, and a good one. Thank you, {player}. Do sit, the tortoise is off duty.

regulars.name: Lloyd Handfield
regulars.hint: Lloyd says a bonefish from the flats is the one fish the whole island respects.
intro: Lloyd: Lloyd. Keeper. Take a seat in the shade. The wind will still be there when you are ready. It always is.
Lloyd: If you chance on a bonefish from the flats, bring it by. That is a fish with manners. It slips away and says nothing.
meet: Lloyd is on a Grand Cayman beach, sandals in hand, looking at the sunset as though checking it against his own.
Lloyd: Over to see friends. Different sea, same blue tablecloth. I hold it up against mine, just to be sure.
Lloyd: Mine is better, but I would not say that to anyone here.
letter: The salt ponds are shining and the wind is brisk. I climbed up this morning and saw the whole island, the town, the reef, and the blue tablecloth laid out for supper. Mind the wind if you visit. It borrows hats.
offer: Lloyd: I have kept a light for ships for years. A business I can mind with half an eye, while the other half watches the horizon.
Lloyd: Go on your walking, {player}. I will be steady, I promise. Wind permitting.
chat: Lloyd: Cast iron, shipped over from England in pieces. Built to last, and it has.
Lloyd: The reef is out there for ships to avoid. They do not always listen.
Lloyd: The salt ponds are glass today. Tomorrow they will look like something else.
thanks: Lloyd turns the bonefish in his hands, silver and long, and smiles as at an old friend.
Lloyd: That is a fine one, {player}. Thank you. Sit down, the wind is gentle for once.

regulars.name: Desmond Wylie
regulars.hint: Mr Wylie says nothing sets him up for a six o'clock start at the window like a proper Ulster fry.
intro: Mr Wylie: Mind the floorboard, it creaks, and the heron hears it. Wylie, Desmond Wylie. Forty years at this window and I have missed only the interesting bits.
Mr Wylie: Early starts are the whole trick. Dawn, binoculars, then breakfast. A proper Ulster fry, soda and potato bread included, and I will let you have the good chair.
meet: Mr Wylie is on a bench in Belfast with his binoculars trained on a gull on a lamp post, notebook open.
Mr Wylie: A common gull, I am told. It is behaving very uncommonly. Visiting my sister. She says I am not to bird in her house, so here we are.
letter: The heron did the same thing again this morning, at the same time, from the same stone. I have written it down for the four thousandth time. I still enjoy it. Come and wait with me.
offer: Mr Wylie: Now, {player}. You want someone to mind that business of yours while you walk. I can sit still for six hours and notice everything that comes through the door.
Mr Wylie: I will not leave the till. Not even for a heron. Possibly for a very good heron.
chat: Mr Wylie: Wait, wait. There. No, gone. That is how it goes.
Mr Wylie: The binoculars are by the window. Do not touch the focus, I have it just so.
Mr Wylie: Dunluce is west along the coast. The cook has never been found. I have my theories.
thanks: Mr Wylie lays the fry down on the sill, then moves his binoculars so they do not get grease on them.
Mr Wylie: That is a breakfast. Five stars. I would write it in the notebook, but my hands are full.

regulars.name: Breda Lynch
regulars.hint: Mrs Lynch says a bowl of colcannon with the butter melting in a well in the middle is the only answer to a Cork November.
intro: Mrs Lynch: Sit down there, you are making the place untidy standing. Breda, I am. You will not remember it, so call me Mrs Lynch like everyone else does.
Mrs Lynch: I will tell you what I like, and then you will know. A good bowl of colcannon, butter pooling in the middle. My husband makes it and then eats half of it before it gets to the table.
meet: Mrs Lynch is on the Kilkenny side of a hurling pitch wearing red, with a flask and a look of grim contentment.
Mrs Lynch: Mrs Lynch: I am surrounded by black and amber and I will not be moved. My husband is gas, he brought a sandwich for each of the three possible results. Sit down, mind my flask.
letter: My son was a header again this week and I have decided to be proud of it. The salmon are back in the Lee, still not asking for directions, and I do admire that in anything. Call in. The kettle is up.
offer: Mrs Lynch: Now {player}, that business of yours. You cannot be walking about the country and minding it. Give it to me. I have run a house with a gas husband and a header son.
Mrs Lynch: A till is nothing after that.
chat: Mrs Lynch: My husband says he will fix the gate. I have put it on the list under 'miracles'.
Mrs Lynch: A header is only a lovely lad with the brakes off. He will settle. I did, I think.
Mrs Lynch: If the Hushwing is out tonight, keep your voice down. The poor creature has enough to put up with.
thanks: Mrs Lynch lifts the lid, breathes in, and says nothing for a good three seconds.
Mrs Lynch: Mrs Lynch: Oh, you good thing. The butter is in the middle where it belongs. Sit, sit, you have earned the good chair.

regulars.name: Francie Brogan
regulars.hint: Mr Brogan says that in all his years on the Foyle he has never landed a salmon, and would not say no to meeting one.
intro: Mr Brogan: Brogan. Francie, if you must. Forty years on this river and I have a great many opinions about it, and no salmon.
Mr Brogan: I do not catch them and they do not catch me. But I would like to see one up close, just the once, in my own kitchen. Bring me an Atlantic salmon and we will call it even.
meet: Mr Brogan is on the Enniskillen shore of Lough Erne, holding a rod with great composure and no bait.
Mr Brogan: Mr Brogan: Different water. Same result. I am told there is a very large fish in there. I thought we might have a chat.
letter: The Foyle went out for a walk at four and came back at ten. That is all the news. I sat there the entire time and the salmon, to a fish, held to our understanding. It is very restful.
offer: Mr Brogan: I have a view on your business. It is that it wants minding. I am a very patient man. I have sat over the Foyle for forty years waiting on a salmon.
Mr Brogan: No customer will beat that.
chat: Mr Brogan: The seals were out at the estuary again. Polite. They tip their heads at you, like a priest.
Mr Brogan: Tide is out. It will be back. It always says it will.
Mr Brogan: Never trust a man who tells you he has caught three salmon. Trust him who tells you none.
thanks: Mr Brogan looks at the salmon for a long, quiet moment, like a man shaking hands with an old rival.
Mr Brogan: Mr Brogan: Well. So that is what they look like. I will say it, it is very well made.

regulars.name: Mattie Flaherty
regulars.hint: Old Mattie says a herring, fresh and fried in butter, is what the old Claddagh men would have called a good dinner and no complaints.
intro: Old Mattie: Ah, come in, come in, will you mind the net, it's drying, or it was meant to be. Mattie, they call me, Old Mattie, since I was about forty.
Old Mattie: My father fished, and his father before him, and they ate herring and thought nothing of it. Bring me a fresh one and I'll fry it up and tell you about the King of the Claddagh.
meet: Old Mattie is on the pier in Dingle, supervising a boat that is not his.

Old Mattie: Old Mattie: Ah, there you are, that's a lovely boat, isn't it. A man here owes me a favour and I'm collecting it in advice. Sit down, will you, I'll tell you about the time I went out in worse than this.
letter: The view out the window is as long as ever and the water as wet. I saw a Pierlord on the wall yesterday and said nothing, as agreed. Bring a herring and I'll tell you the whole story, twice.
Yours, Mattie (Old, though I've been told not to say so)
offer: Old Mattie: Now, {player}, I've been thinking about that business of yours, and a man has to do something, and I've mended nets and kept a quay and I'd mind it.
Old Mattie: Go on away walking, I'll keep the place afloat. Mostly.
chat: Old Mattie: The wind is coming round to the west. A good sign or a bad one, depending on who's asking.
Old Mattie: They cleared the cottages, but they couldn't clear the view. I still have it.
Old Mattie: Keep the sandwich in the bag. That's all I'll say about the Pierlords.
thanks: Old Mattie holds the herring up to the window, like a man checking a banknote.
Old Mattie: Old Mattie: Oh, that's grand, that's a beauty, silver as a new coin. My father would have wept. He'd have said it was too small, but he'd have wept.

regulars.name: Nora Daly
regulars.hint: Gran Daly says a warm soda bread with plenty of butter is the only fuel a Kilkenny supporter needs for a big match.
intro: Gran Daly: Sit, sit, not on the hurley. Nora Daly, though it's Gran Daly to the whole street and half the county. Touch the hurley, it does no harm.
Gran Daly: Now, I'll tell you what gets me through a final. A good soda bread, warm, butter on it thick as a slate. Bring me one and I'll say a prayer for the Cats and a second one for you.
meet: Gran Daly is in a Dublin street on the day of a big match, in black and amber, carrying a hurley she is absolutely not meant to have.
Gran Daly: Gran Daly: Do not look at the hurley. It's for luck, it's not for use. Well, mostly. Good to see you, now off, I've a match to win.
letter: The hurley is still over the fire and I touch it going past, whether it's working or not. It is lashing rain, so I have not left the kitchen. Come in and sit, and bring a loaf if you're passing.
Yours, Nora (Gran Daly, to the Cats)
offer: Gran Daly: Now, {player}. That business of yours wants someone with a bit of sense and a loud voice. I have both. I raised a hurling team, practically, and some of them were mine.
Gran Daly: I will run it. Bring the key and go.
chat: Gran Daly: Two hares boxing in the field this morning. The lady won. They always know.
Gran Daly: I am not nervous about Sunday. I have only been sitting by the radio since Tuesday.
Gran Daly: Mind yourself on the wet road. 'Tis lashing again, and not the generous way.
thanks: Gran Daly breaks off a corner, butters it, and eats it standing up, which she never does.
Gran Daly: Gran Daly: Ah, that is the right one. Warm. You are a good child. Come here to me.

regulars.name: Aidan Hannon
regulars.hint: Mr Hannon says a Shannon salmon, plainly done, is the only dish fit to be served in a Georgian dining room.
intro: Mr Hannon: Hannon, Aidan Hannon. I would show you the ballroom, but there are four storeys of stairs between us and I do not trust my knees. Sit, sit. The fox will not mind.
Mr Hannon: If you ever pass a good Atlantic salmon, I would be glad of one. The Shannon is only down the road, and a salmon in this house does feel as though it has come home.
meet: Mr Hannon is in Cork in the foyer of a theatre, wearing a very good coat and the expression of a man guarding it.
Mr Hannon: Mr Hannon: You find me away from the ballroom. A cousin has a play on, and the foyer, I am pleased to say, is not as grand as mine. Good to see you. Say nothing to the cousin.
letter: The Georgian windows have been cleaned and the fox has been on the good rug again. I have stopped arguing. It sits better than I do. Come by and I shall give you the proper tour, all four storeys.
offer: Mr Hannon: Now {player}. A business wants a steady hand and a good eye for a draught. I have kept four storeys of tall windows closed against a Limerick winter.
Mr Hannon: I can manage a till. It has only one floor.
chat: Mr Hannon: Frank McCourt was a mile from here and a world away. I say it to everyone. I think he would have found it funny.
Mr Hannon: The fanlights were put in to catch the light. They catch the dust too.
Mr Hannon: The fox is not a pet. He does not think so either.
thanks: Mr Hannon looks at the salmon as though it were about to be presented at court.
Mr Hannon: Mr Hannon: Well. We shall have it plain, with a little parsley, in the dining room. The fox may watch from the door.

regulars.name: Ruth Gannon
regulars.hint: Ruth says a bowl of champ with a well of butter in the middle is the only thing that gets her through a wet day in a trench.
intro: Ruth: Ruth Gannon. Yes, the one who stayed. Fifteen years of a summer dig. The soil does not forgive you for leaving a trowel in it.
Ruth: If you want to thank me for the tour, the best thing is a bowl of champ, scallions, butter, plenty of salt. It is the only decent thing to come out of a wet trench.
meet: Ruth is in Sligo, kneeling at the edge of a prehistoric tomb with her notebook on her knee and a flask on the ground.
Ruth: Ruth: Carrowmore, my day off. I came to look at stones, because apparently I do not get enough of that. Do not tell my supervisor I am enjoying it.
letter: Another summer, another trench, another beautiful pile of nothing in particular. Someone found a flint. We held a small, dignified party. The soil remembers everything, and I am trying to be a better listener.
offer: Ruth: Now, {player}. I have catalogued ten thousand shards of pottery. A till is not going to trouble me.
Ruth: I label everything. I will keep your shop in order, whether it asks me to or not.
chat: Ruth: We found a spiral today. It is a very good spiral. Nobody has told us what it means, so I have decided it means 'hello'.
Ruth: The Pooka are out tonight, they say. I will keep my blackberries in the cupboard.
Ruth: Fifteen years and I am still the new girl. That is how it works around here.
thanks: Ruth takes the champ and breathes in, the steam fogging her glasses.
Ruth: Ruth: Oh, that is exactly right. I will log it. Find number one. Context, my kitchen. Condition, vanishing.

regulars.name: Con Moriarty
regulars.hint: Old Con says a pot of Irish stew, with the lamb and the potatoes and nothing clever, is all a man needs after a day on the hill.
intro: Old Con: Come in, sit down. Con Moriarty. Old Con, they say, though I was Young Con for a long time and it passed without ceremony. Sure look it.
Old Con: I do like a stew. Lamb, potatoes, onion, nothing clever. Bring me a pot of it and I will tell you the whole of Daniel O'Connell, and you can say 'who?' if you like.
meet: Old Con is at Galway Races with a flat cap, a very small bet and a face of complete calm.
Old Con: Old Con: I have a horse. I have not told it. Sure look it, it is only a bit of fun. You will not tell the wife.
letter: The stags are roaring on the hill and the Fawnlets are hiding in the bracken, and I am sitting here with a cup of tea, watching it all go on without me. Sure look it. Come down for the stew.
offer: Old Con: Now {player}. About that business of yours. Somebody has to mind it. I have minded cattle, sheep and a mother-in-law.
Old Con: Sure look it, a till is nothing to that.
chat: Old Con: Sure look it. That is the answer. I never needed another.
Old Con: The rain is on the hills. It will be on the hills tomorrow. It is a very loyal rain.
Old Con: O'Connell was born near Cahersiveen. Say that, and someone says 'who?'. It is a great game.
thanks: Old Con lifts the lid, sniffs, and puts the lid back with a look of deep respect.
Old Con: Old Con: That is a stew. No nonsense in it. Well, sure look it, you did well.

regulars.name: Batt Considine
regulars.hint: Old Batt says an eel from the Shannon, done the old way, is a dish his father would have called a feast.
intro: Old Batt: Sit in, sit in. Batt Considine, they say, Old Batt now, since I got to a certain age. That is the settle bed, and I will not discuss who lost the argument.
Old Batt: If you are ever passing the river, I would not say no to an eel out of the Shannon. A dish my father loved, and my father had opinions.
meet: Old Batt is wandering the stalls in Limerick, tasting nothing, buying nothing, and thoroughly enjoying himself.
Old Batt: Old Batt: A market is a great thing for the soul. You look at it all and you buy a single onion. Come back to the cottage some day. The kettle is on the crane.
letter: The fire is lit and has been lit since morning. It will be lit after. I raked it over last night and blew it back to life, as is right. The half-door is open on top and shut below. The hens are furious.
offer: Old Batt: Now {player}, listen. That business of yours. I have run a farm, a half-door and a houseful of children. A till does not frighten me.
Old Batt: Give me the key. I will mind it by the fire, mostly.
chat: Old Batt: The hens are in a mood. I would not go near them, and they would not thank you.
Old Batt: They say the fire never went out for two hundred years. I do not doubt it. It would not dare.
Old Batt: The settle goes from bench to bed. The child who lost the argument goes with it.
thanks: Old Batt takes the eel and holds it up to the firelight like a man appraising a good horse.
Old Batt: Old Batt: Well now. That is a Shannon eel, all right. My father would have taken his hat off to it.

regulars.name: Peggy McGowan
regulars.hint: Nana says a boxty off the griddle, with butter, is the only thing that makes her stop giving out.
intro: Nana: Sit down, sit down, you are blocking the light. Peggy McGowan, though it is Nana to everyone, even the postman. I give out about the weather, I give out about the postman, I am very well.
Nana: I do like a boxty off the griddle, with a bit of butter on it. Bring me one and I will give out a good deal less.
meet: Nana is on a bench in Donegal Town, looking at the sky with an expression of deep personal disappointment.
Nana: Nana: My sister lives here and the weather is even worse. I am delighted. Have you ever seen such a sky? I have a list. Sit down, it is a long list.
letter: I have given out about the weather since 1971 and I see no reason to stop now. The Brocklings were in the garden again, behaving. The bins stayed shut. We are at peace. Come and have a cup of tea before the next shower.
offer: Nana: Now, {player}. That business of yours wants a woman who gives out properly. I have given out to bank managers, bishops and a very stubborn goat.
Nana: Hand it over. I will have it shipshape in a week, and I will say so.
chat: Nana: It is raining. I will say no more. I will say a great deal more, but not yet.
Nana: The kettle forgave me again this morning. It is a very generous kettle.
Nana: Keep the bins shut. The Brocklings will know. They always know.
thanks: Nana turns the boxty over on the plate, sniffs, and gives an approving little nod.
Nana: Nana: Well, I will not say a word. That is a lovely one. I will say nothing at all. Sit down, I will pour you tea.

regulars.name: Alec Duthie
regulars.hint: Mr Duthie says a good haddock is the only thing that ever made a council meeting feel worth the wait.
intro: Mr Duthie: Alec Duthie, Clerk to nobody in particular. I have minuted forty years of meetings and the only decision anyone remembers is the biscuits.
Mr Duthie: Bon Accord, as the motto says, which is more than I can say for the agenda. Bring me a haddock some day and I will read you the good minutes.
meet: Mr Duthie is on a Dundee pavement holding a lanyard and a sandwich, looking like a man who escaped a conference.
Mr Duthie: Clerks' day out. Four hours on procedure. I have taken minutes of my own lunch to cope.
Mr Duthie: Good to see you. Aberdeen is the one with the granite, in case you wander off.
letter: The landing is quiet this week. The councillors are not as fast as they look, but they have found the tea trolley at last. I have minuted the occasion.
offer: Mr Duthie: A word, {player}. Your business wants someone with a steady hand and a filing system while you are off walking.
Mr Duthie: I have kept order among councillors. A till is very polite by comparison.
chat: Mr Duthie: Item one, the weather. Item two, more weather. Carried.
Mr Duthie: Granite does not change its mind. I find that restful.
Mr Duthie: Three towers and two leopards on the arms. I have counted them twice, in case they moved.
thanks: Mr Duthie holds the haddock at arm's length, as if reviewing it.
Mr Duthie: Approved without amendment. I shall not minute that I am delighted.

regulars.name: Morag Henderson
regulars.hint: Mrs Henderson says a pot of stovies is the proper answer to any haar.
intro: Mrs Henderson: Come in, dear, before the haar takes you. Morag Henderson, though everyone says Mrs Henderson, even my grandson.
Mrs Henderson: I make my stovies in a heavy pot and they cure most things. Bring me a plate of them and I will tell you what the Castle really does at night.
meet: Mrs Henderson is on a Glasgow platform with a tartan bag the size of a toddler, scanning the crowd.
Mrs Henderson: My daughter stays here. Nice people, but they walk too fast and they say hen to me, and I am old enough to be several hens.
Mrs Henderson: Away you go, and mind the haar when you are back in Edinburgh.
letter: My wee grandson has decided the Castle follows him to school as well. I have told him it is just very tall. He says that is what the Castle wants us to think.
Yours, Morag (Mrs Henderson, to the grandchildren)
offer: Mrs Henderson: Now then, {player}. Your business wants someone with a firm hand and a pot of something hot on the go.
Mrs Henderson: I have raised a family and survived a Fringe. I can manage customers.
chat: Mrs Henderson: The haar was in all morning. I could not see my own scone, so I ate it to be safe.
Mrs Henderson: The hootlets were at it again last night. Twit-twoo. They are in charge, I told you.
Mrs Henderson: My grandson says the Castle is following him. I have stopped arguing.
thanks: Mrs Henderson lifts the lid, breathes in and closes her eyes for a moment.
Mrs Henderson: Oh, that will do nicely. You are a good soul, and do not let the haar tell you otherwise.

regulars.name: Calum Munro
regulars.hint: Old Calum says a salmon from a Highland river is the only fish he would walk a mile in the rain to look at.
intro: Old Calum: Quiet, now. You will frighten the river. Calum, they call me Old Calum, I am told it is respect.
Old Calum: Forty years I have stood in cold water telling gentlemen to lift the rod. Bring me a salmon and I will say very little about it, which is the highest praise.
meet: Old Calum is outside a Fort William outdoor shop, holding a pair of waders up to the light.
Old Calum: Ben Nevis is behind us. I am not looking at it. I have an arrangement with that hill.
Old Calum: Good to see you. Find a river on your way back, and do not splash.
letter: The river is up and the gentlemen are down, which is the right way round. I have said nothing for three days and I feel very well on it.
offer: Old Calum: You, {player}. Your business wants someone who can stand still and watch for trouble.
Old Calum: I can do that for eleven hours without a flask. Give me the flask as well.
chat: Old Calum: The water is low. I have mentioned it to the sky.
Old Calum: A good fish is patient. So am I, mostly.
Old Calum: Lift the rod, you said. I did not say it twice.
thanks: Old Calum weighs the salmon in one hand and nods once, slowly.
Old Calum: Aye. That is a fish. I will say no more, and I mean it kindly.

regulars.name: Magnus Flett
regulars.hint: Magnus says a herring, salted or fresh, is the only fish a good story should be served alongside.
intro: Magnus: Sit down, sit down. Magnus Flett, and yes, there are a great many Fletts in Orkney, and most of us tell stories.
Magnus: A story is better on a full stomach. Bring me a herring some day and I will tell you one about the selkie that was not even a good swimmer.
meet: Magnus is at Thurso with a rucksack, having come across the Pentland Firth on the boat and looking mildly betrayed by the sea.
Magnus: The firth was in a mood. I told it a story about a fisherman who talked too much, and it stopped. Mostly.
Magnus: Good to see you. Kirkwall is the one with the big red cathedral. You cannot miss it, though you will try.
letter: A new tale this week, of a man who took a boat out and came back with a sea-view and no fish. I told it in the shop and now everyone has an opinion.
offer: Magnus: I have an idea, {player}. Your business wants a person who can keep customers while the owner is off walking.
Magnus: I can talk to anyone for an hour. It is selling that I will have to learn.
chat: Magnus: I have a story for it, whatever the weather. That is not a boast, it is a warning.
Magnus: A good tale gets better each telling. A poor one gets longer.
Magnus: The sea has been rude again. I put it in the next one.
thanks: Magnus looks at the herring and begins to smile, slowly.
Magnus: Now that is a worthy fish. I will tell you a tale about it, but you will owe me another.

regulars.name: Tammie Isbister
regulars.hint: Old Tammie says nothing helps a fiddler's wrist like a fresh mackerel and a long sit down.
intro: Old Tammie: Sixty years, I said. Maybe sixty-one. The fiddle does not mind and neither do I.
Old Tammie: Tammie Isbister, though everyone says Old Tammie. If you ever catch a mackerel, bring it to me and I will play you a reel, a short one.
meet: Old Tammie is on the Aberdeen quay, fiddle case under his arm, looking at the NorthLink boat like a hall that has promised a wedding.
Old Tammie: A christening at Torry, they said. In a gale, I said. Sixty years and nothing changes.
Old Tammie: Good to see you. Come back to Lerwick when you can. The tune is waiting.
