letter: I played at a wedding last Saturday. The bride was danced off her feet, so it was not a poor do. I may have broken a string, but only in the good bit.
offer: Old Tammie: I will be plain, {player}. Your business needs someone to mind it while you are walking.
Old Tammie: I have kept a hall dancing all night. A shop is a doddle.
chat: Old Tammie: A reel is only a story with its feet moving.
Old Tammie: Granny said the best tunes came from the sea. It is a lie, I think. I still use it.
Old Tammie: My bow arm is better than yesterday. My knees are a different matter.
thanks: Old Tammie turns the mackerel over, tapping it like a tuning fork.
Old Tammie: Well now. That deserves a tune. Sit down, and do not talk through the slow part.

regulars.name: Ina Sinclair
regulars.hint: Mrs Sinclair says a plate of queenie scallops is the only thing that makes the last cup of tea on the mainland feel like a send-off.
intro: Mrs Sinclair: Welcome in. Ina Sinclair, though the postcards only know me as the Shopkeeper.
Mrs Sinclair: I would be glad of a few queenie scallops one day. Bring some, and I will do you the very last cup of tea, with a flourish.
meet: Mrs Sinclair is in Kirkwall, standing at a shop window with a bag of postcards, comparing prices.
Mrs Sinclair: Market research. Their postcards are nicer than mine. I am furious, and I am buying six.
Mrs Sinclair: Good to see you. Do come back to the Last House. Nobody counts Dunnet Head.
letter: A coach party came through on Tuesday and bought forty postcards and no tea. I have not forgiven them. The groatie buckies are selling well, though.
Yours, Ina (Sinclair, last of the mainland)
offer: Mrs Sinclair: Listen, {player}. Your business wants someone who can keep a till and a smile, at the end of the road.
Mrs Sinclair: I have sold tea at the last house for years. Everything else is easy.
chat: Mrs Sinclair: Haste ye back, I say, and I mean it, whatever the wind is doing.
Mrs Sinclair: Nobody counts Dunnet Head. I do, quietly.
Mrs Sinclair: The tea is hot, the postcards are damp and the view is free.
thanks: Mrs Sinclair peers into the bag with the air of a woman checking a ledger.
Mrs Sinclair: Oh, they are lovely. You have just made my week, and I will not tell the coach party.

regulars.name: Ishbel Gunn
regulars.hint: Granny Gunn says a smokie is the only thing that tastes of a good fire and a bad winter in one go.
intro: Granny Gunn: Come in, come in, mind the cat. Ishbel Gunn, though nobody has said it aloud since 1971.
Granny Gunn: I am fond of a smokie, with a bit of bread. Bring me one and I will not say you have had your tea.
meet: Granny Gunn is outside Raigmore Hospital in Inverness with a flask, a knitting bag and a grudge about the car park.
Granny Gunn: Appointment. Perfectly fine. They tell me I am perfectly fine and charge me for the parking, which is not fine.
Granny Gunn: Good to see you. Get home to Thurso and keep the cat company.
letter: The Keiths have been mentioned at the church again. I have said nothing, loudly. The cat is well and sends nothing, as is her way.
Yours, Ishbel (Gunn, and proud of it)
offer: Granny Gunn: Now, {player}. Your business wants someone with Gunn blood and a kettle to keep it going.
Granny Gunn: We kept a feud going for centuries. A shop is nothing.
chat: Granny Gunn: The flagstones held the heat again. Stone does, you see.
Granny Gunn: Have a crowdie oatcake. No? Aye, you will have had your tea.
Granny Gunn: Norse blood, I told you. It does not wash out, though the Keiths tried.
thanks: Granny Gunn sniffs the smokie and nods like an old friend has called.
Granny Gunn: Now that is a fish. Sit down, you will have a cup of tea. You have not had your tea.

regulars.name: Murdo Macleod
regulars.hint: Murdo says a clootie dumpling is the proper answer to a long, damp afternoon beside a peat fire.
intro: Murdo: Fàilte. Murdo Macleod, who shows folk around a house his granny would not have let them into without wiping their feet.
Murdo: A clootie dumpling would be very welcome beside the fire. Bring one, and I will say tapadh leibh, and mean it.
meet: Murdo is on the Stornoway waterfront with an empty rucksack and the happy face of a man who has left his group behind.
Murdo: A day off from the black house. Peat all week and now I find I am looking for a hill to stand on.
Murdo: Good to see you. Come back to Harris. We promised not to tell the visitors about the chimney.
letter: The visitors asked again whether the cattle really helped heat the house. I said yes, and they looked at the sofa in the next room with a new respect.
Yours, Murdo (Macleod, guide and chimney sweep)
offer: Murdo: A thought, {player}. Your business wants someone steady while you are away walking.
Murdo: I keep a house of strangers warm and informed. A shop is smaller than a black house.
chat: Murdo: The smoke says it is cold, and it is.
Murdo: My granny read the weather in the peat reek. She was right more than the forecast.
Murdo: Gearrannan is quiet today. The wind has taken the rest.
thanks: Murdo lifts the cloth and the warm smell of spice and fruit fills the room.
Murdo: Ah, now. That is a proper one. Tapadh leibh, and sit down by the fire.

regulars.name: Ma Haig
regulars.hint: Ma Haig says nobody bakes well on an empty stomach, and a bowl of Scotch broth is how she starts the day.
intro: Ma Haig: Come in, hen, come in. Ma Haig, to the whole town, and my own mother called me worse.
Ma Haig: I am up at four with the ovens. A bowl of Scotch broth sets me up for the day, so if you have one, I will not say no.
meet: Ma Haig is on a Waverley platform with a basket of bannocks, guarding it like a Reiver's loot.
Ma Haig: Wholesaler's meeting. They offered me a sandwich. I laughed so hard they gave me a second one.
Ma Haig: Good to see you. Get yourself to the Borders. The bakehouse is warm and the Common Riding is coming.
letter: The Selkirk bannock is going like the clappers. A woman from Hawick tried to say it was not the best in the Borders, and she has not been back since.
offer: Ma Haig: Now then, {player}. Your business wants a firm hand and a hot oven. I am both.
Ma Haig: I have fed half the Borders. Folk who pay cash are a pleasure.
chat: Ma Haig: The bannock is good, and so are you, and so is the pie. Eat.
Ma Haig: A pie that would stop a Reiver at forty paces. I have tested it, forty-one in fact.
Ma Haig: Mind the steps. The town is hungry again.
thanks: Ma Haig lifts the lid, inhales and nods slowly, as if inspecting a rival bakery.
Ma Haig: Well. That is a decent pot. You can come in any time, hen.

regulars.name: Idris Lloyd
regulars.hint: Idris says a fresh mackerel from the bay is the nearest he gets to rowing out before dawn these days.
intro: Idris: I used to row out of this harbour before dawn. Mair says I still do, in my sleep, and that I steer badly.
Idris: A fresh mackerel from the bay would make an old man feel useful. Bring me one and I will tell the tide you said hello.
meet: Idris is on Aberdeen harbour, studying a trawler with the air of a man doing a stock check.
Idris: Mair said I should get out of the house. I said I would go to the harbour. She did not specify which one.
Idris: I have eleven boats in bottles at home. This one is full size. The scale is much better.
letter: Mair says the new coat is a coat and not a sail. I have tested it on the harbour wall and the jury is out. The bottle count stands at twelve, and I am not discussing it.
offer: Idris: I have been getting up before dawn for years, even if I mostly say so now. A business at eight o'clock holds no terrors.
Idris: Leave it with me, {player}. I will count the takings. Mair will count them again.
chat: Idris: The Ystwyth and the Rheidol are arguing again. The tide is taking notes.
Idris: Number thirteen has a very small anchor. I am quietly proud of it.
Idris: Mair says I talk to the boats. They never answer back, which I find restful.
thanks: Idris holds the mackerel up to the light as if it were the last of the morning.
Idris: Now that is a proper fish. I will say I caught it. Mair will say I did not. We will both be right.

regulars.name: Nain Olwen
regulars.hint: Nain says a warm Welsh cake straight off the bakestone settles a tamping temper, a wispet fright and most other things.
intro: Nain: Sit, cariad, and do not mind the cat, he thinks he owns that chair. I am Nain to everybody, even the postman, and he is forty.
Nain: I would be glad of a Welsh cake, if you come across one. A warm one, mind. A cold one is only a biscuit with ideas.
meet: Nain is on the Holyhead quay with a flask and a tartan blanket, watching the Irish ferry as if it owes her money.
Nain: Our Sioned says I should not wait for ferries. I am not waiting, cariad. I am supervising.
Nain: Come back to the cottage for tea. The wispets are out along the hedge at dusk and they do like an audience.
letter: Sioned still says the long village name was a stunt. I told her stunts are how people find us, and she went quiet, which is rare. The cat sends a look. Come for a Welsh cake.
offer: Nain: I have run a kitchen, a family and a very opinionated cat. Your business will be no trouble, cariad.
Nain: Go and walk, {player}. I will put a Welsh cake in the till and a warning on the door.
chat: Nain: A tamping temper is only hunger with a loud voice. Feed it and it passes.
Nain: Wispets were bobbing along the hedge again last night, showy as ever.
Nain: Sioned calls the long name a stunt. I call it a very long welcome mat.
thanks: Nain takes the Welsh cake in both hands and holds it to her cheek like a hot water bottle.
Nain: Still warm. You have the touch, cariad. The cat will want a crumb and he will not get one.

regulars.name: Wilf Bevan
regulars.hint: Old Wilf says a proper Glamorgan sausage, all cheese and leek and not a scrap of meat, was the best thing a dock lunch box ever held.
intro: Old Wilf: Alright, butt. It is Wilf, but everybody says Old Wilf, as if there is a young one hiding round the back. There is not.
Old Wilf: Best lunch I ever had on the docks was a Glamorgan sausage. All cheese and leek. Bring me a home-made one and I will tell you which crane I hated.
meet: Old Wilf is on the Liverpool waterfront, looking at the Mersey like a man checking another man's homework.
Old Wilf: Big docks, Liverpool. Good ones. Do not tell anyone in Cardiff I said so.
Old Wilf: The sandwiches here are rubbish, mind. Come home to Butetown, butt, and I will find you a proper lunch.
letter: The bay is quiet and the gulls are still after my chips. I told one it was a Cardiff gull and ought to know better. Shirley Bassey would have handled it with style. I handle it with a newspaper.
offer: Old Wilf: Forty years I moved cargo from every corner of the world. A till and a queue will not trouble me, butt.
Old Wilf: Go and walk. I will keep the stock moving and the gulls out.
chat: Old Wilf: Sailors came from everywhere to this bay. Everyone left something behind, mostly recipes and arguments.
Old Wilf: Mind the gulls, butt. They watch the dock like a union.
Old Wilf: Tiger Bay, they called it. We called it home. Still do.
thanks: Old Wilf unwraps the Glamorgan sausage and sniffs it like a customs officer.
Old Wilf: Leek, cheese, crisp outside. Cleared for landing. Diolch, butt.

regulars.name: Emrys Roberts
regulars.hint: Emrys says nothing warmed a quarryman through a long shift like a bowl of cawl, and he has not found anything better since.
intro: Emrys: Emrys is the name. I was at Dinorwic until it closed in 1969, and my back has been sending the bill ever since.
Emrys: Cawl is what kept us going up there. Bring me a bowl, home-made, and I will tell you where the good slate was.
meet: Emrys is standing in a Llangollen street with his neck tipped back, staring at somebody's roof.
Emrys: Welsh slate. You can tell by the way it sits. Proud, like. Do not tell me it is Spanish, I will sit down and sulk.
Emrys: Someone is going to say it came off a church hall in Leeds. It might be mine. I stopped counting years ago.
letter: The slatelets are about on the spoil heaps again, treating the whole quarry as a playground. I was never allowed to. I was paid to. Bring cawl, or at the very least an appetite.
offer: Emrys: I worked beside thousands of men at Dinorwic, give or take. A stall and a queue are a quiet afternoon.
Emrys: Go and walk, {player}. I will keep the books straight and the slate dry.
chat: Emrys: Bryn Eglwys means church hill. The church has gone and the hill stayed. That is the Welsh way.
Emrys: Half the roofs in Britain, and nobody ever thanks the slate.
Emrys: Stand still on the spoil heap and a slatelet will come and look at you. Rude, but honest.
thanks: Emrys lifts the lid and breathes in as if it were mountain air.
Emrys: Cawl. Proper cawl. Diolch, {player}. You have the hands of a quarry wife and I mean that as the highest praise.

regulars.name: Menna Rees
regulars.hint: Mrs Rees says a pollack off the Strumble rocks, fried in butter, is the only dinner worth the walk back from the headland.
intro: Mrs Rees: I am Mrs Rees, though out here it is mostly 'is there tea'. Mind the wind, it does for hairdos and for opinions.
Mrs Rees: Four flashes every fifteen seconds and I count along. Bring me a pollack off the rocks and I will count you as a friend.
meet: Mrs Rees is outside the cathedral in St Davids, wearing a red shawl and looking a little too pleased with herself.
Mrs Rees: Do not laugh. The women at Fishguard wore red in 1797 and the French went home. I am only keeping up the family business.
Mrs Rees: Come out to Strumble when you can. The lighthouse is just across the footbridge and the kettle is always on.
letter: The light flashed its four every fifteen seconds all night and I counted along, as ever. The child waved at the Irish ferry and still nobody waved back. I have started waving for them.
offer: Mrs Rees: I have kept house on a headland through every gale going. A business is a breeze.
Mrs Rees: I will keep the light on for you, {player}. Figuratively. The real one does it by itself.
chat: Mrs Rees: The wind did for my hairdo again. I am told it is a look.
Mrs Rees: The Irish ferry went by at noon. The child waved. Nobody waved back. It is becoming a tradition.
Mrs Rees: The French mistook the women for soldiers in 1797. Fishguard has never been prouder or less surprised.
thanks: Mrs Rees takes the pollack and weighs it in her palm like a woman who has seen many fish and been fooled by few.
Mrs Rees: A beauty. That is dinner and a story, {player}. The French would have surrendered over less.

regulars.name: Dilys Morgan
regulars.hint: Dilys says nothing beats a Welsh cake still warm from the range, eaten in the kitchen and never the parlour.
intro: Dilys: Come in, cariad, mind the step, it is high, I told the vicar and he fell anyway. I am Dilys, Mrs Pugh's sister, which is a full-time job.
Dilys: If you ever have a Welsh cake going, a warm one, I would be glad of it. Kitchen, mind. Nobody is allowed in the parlour.
meet: Dilys is outside Big Pit in Blaenavon, in a hard hat, which she is wearing over her good hat.
Dilys: They take you down in a cage, cariad. I said I would, then I said I would not, and now I am a woman who has done it.
Dilys: Down there they have a lamp and no parlour at all. Imagine.
letter: The tin bath is still on its nail, the good clock is still ticking in the parlour, and nobody is still allowed in. I put the kettle on in the kitchen like everybody else. Come and sit.
offer: Dilys: I fed a house full of men off one range and a lot of opinions. Your business is a Tuesday, cariad.
Dilys: Go on, off you walk. I will keep the accounts and the best china, and I will not let anyone in the parlour.
chat: Dilys: Friday was bath night. You always wanted to be first, the water gets a grey look after the fifth man.
Dilys: They built the fireplace first and the house round it. Priorities, cariad.
Dilys: The good clock is in the parlour and it tells the time to nobody. Very dignified.
thanks: Dilys holds the Welsh cake in a tea towel as if it were a small, golden, sleeping baby.
Dilys: Still warm! Not the parlour, mind, we will eat this at the kitchen table like normal people. Diolch, cariad.

regulars.name: Emlyn Griffiths
regulars.hint: Mr Griffiths says laverbread on hot toast is just what a man wants after a cold morning on the sound.
intro: Mr Griffiths: Griffiths, and if you say Mister I will turn round to look for my father. That is Ramsey Island in the window. Ynys Dewi to the saint.
Mr Griffiths: Home-made laverbread on hot toast is what a man wants after a cold morning on the sound. Bring me some and I will show you where the seals pup.
meet: Mr Griffiths is at Swansea Market, quietly arguing with a stallholder about the price of cockles.
Mr Griffiths: Laverbread is fine here, but the woman at the second stall will not tell me where she gets it. I respect that. I hate it.
Mr Griffiths: Do not tell Mrs Griffiths I am here. She thinks I am at the harbour. Swansea has one, so I am almost not lying.
letter: The seals are pupping on Ramsey again, white and fluffy and furious, so I give them room and they take it as a compliment. A puffling by the cliff top still has not forgiven me.
offer: Mr Griffiths: I have dealt with tides and gulls all my life. A till is quieter than the sound at spring tide.
Mr Griffiths: Off you go, {player}. I will mind the shop. The gulls will not get past me. Probably.
chat: Mr Griffiths: Ramsey Island is much too small for how dramatic it is. I say so every morning.
Mr Griffiths: Seals on the beaches. Give them room. They are only furious because they are right.
Mr Griffiths: Seren calls it hwyl, when the sea and the choir agree. I call it a good tide.
thanks: Mr Griffiths tips the laverbread onto toast without ceremony and eats it standing at the window.
Mr Griffiths: Ahh. That is the sea in a dish. Diolch, {player}. The seals will hear of this.

regulars.name: Morag Kerr
regulars.hint: Morag says a proper haddock on the plate would settle the argument over who is catching more, her son or his sister.
intro: Morag: Morag. Mind the smirr, it gets in. My boy is learning to bait a hook and his sister is out-fishing him by a mile. He says it is the bait. It is not the bait.
Morag: A haddock would settle the argument and the tea. Bring me one and I will tell you about the ternlets.
meet: Morag is on the Belfast quayside with a carrier bag and the look of a woman on a very rare day off.
Morag: Two hours on the ferry and I am still wearing the smirr. It followed me. Loyal, I suppose.
Morag: Do not tell the children I am enjoying myself. They will want a share.
letter: The path down to the harbour is all glaur again. My boy blames the weather and his sister blames my boy. The ternlets dived at dawn and looked deeply serious about it. I looked serious too and caught nothing.
offer: Morag: I run a house, a boy, his sister and a ferry timetable. A business is simple by comparison.
Morag: Off you go, {player}. I will have it in order and the till full, and nobody will argue.
chat: Morag: Smirr again. You do not see it. You just find you are wearing it.
Morag: My boy swears it is the bait. His sister swears it is skill. I swear I am not getting involved.
Morag: The loch is flat as a plate and the ternlets are hovering. I will be quiet now.
thanks: Morag turns the haddock over and gives it the look she gives a promising knot.
Morag: A proper haddock. Wait until my boy sees it. He will say it is the bait.

regulars.name: Bessie Dunn
regulars.hint: Bessie says a plate of stovies is the stoater a canal boater needs at the end of a long day on the tiller.
intro: Bessie: Bessie. Falkirk bairn, born and bred, and proud of it, which is the only way to be one.
Bessie: A plate of stovies after a day on the water is a stoater. Bring me some, home-made, and I am your friend for life.
meet: Bessie is at the canal basin in Edinburgh, regarding a narrowboat with open professional disapproval.
Bessie: The Union Canal comes all the way from Falkirk to here, and this is where it stops. I just wanted to see it arrive.
Bessie: Edinburgh folk are very nice. They say it as if they were doing you a favour.
letter: A hot roll on a cold morning is a stoater, so I had two, and the cold lost. The bairns are in the canal again, shouting at ducks. I am told they are the neighbours' bairns. I have taken credit.
offer: Bessie: I have worked a lock with half the village watching. A till is a doddle.
Bessie: Away you go and walk, {player}. I will keep the books straight, and anyone who wants to meddle can speak to me.
chat: Bessie: Better meddle wi' the de'il than the bairns o' Falkirk. I said it again only yesterday.
Bessie: A hot roll is a stoater. Two hot rolls is a morning.
Bessie: The canal never hurries. That is why it always arrives.
thanks: Bessie lifts the lid, breathes the steam and closes her eyes like she has just been forgiven.
Bessie: Stovies! That is a stoater, {player}. You have the touch. Sit, and I will tell you who was talking about you.

regulars.name: Isa Brodie
regulars.hint: Granny Isa says a slice of clootie dumpling and a cup of tea is the best reason she knows to sit down for an hour.
intro: Granny Isa: Isa to my pals, Granny Isa to the rest, and Granny to anyone with a parcel. Sit, hen, sit.
Granny Isa: A clootie dumpling with a good skin on it, that is a Sunday. If you ever have one, I will count it as a green place.
meet: Granny Isa is in Dundee, on a bench by the waterfront, eating chips with great dignity and one eye on the sky.
Granny Isa: A friend moved here and I came to see if it is as good as she says. It is. Do not tell her.
Granny Isa: The V and A is lovely and the wind is not. Mind your chips, hen. The gulls are professionals.
letter: I counted the parks on Sunday again and got to ninety-one, which means I have found a new one or counted the bowling green twice. The sootwings are back in the stonework, filthy and unrepentant as ever.
offer: Granny Isa: I have counted ninety parks and never lost one. A wee business of yours is no bother, hen.
Granny Isa: Away you go and walk. I will keep it tidy, and anyone who wants a stooshie can wait in the close.
chat: Granny Isa: Dreich again. I will not complain. I will say it with feeling.
Granny Isa: Sootwings in the stonework. They love a good fog and have never apologised once.
Granny Isa: Put the kettle on and tell me a story. Preferably one about somebody else.
thanks: Granny Isa cuts the clootie dumpling with the solemn care of a woman opening a new bridge.
Granny Isa: That is a skin done right. Ah, hen, you will go far. And you will come back for tea, I hope.

regulars.name: Catriona MacDougall
regulars.hint: Granny says a plate of queenie scallops fresh off the Oban boats would forgive the whole west coast.
intro: Granny: I have watched ferries from this window since 1958. Everybody on them is coming home or running away, and I can tell which.
Granny: A plate of queenies, fresh from the boats, and I would forgive the whole west coast. If you see any, remember an old woman.
meet: Granny is on the front at Tobermory, wrapped in four layers, checking that the painted houses are all still there.
Granny: A ferry, Mull and a coat. That is my holiday. I have been told to relax, so I am doing it at speed.
Granny: Ciamar a tha thu. Do not worry, I will not test you on the spelling.
letter: The ferry came in at ten past four, as it does. A man stood exactly where it was about to go. I will not say who. I told him the first rule of Oban and he was very good about it after.
offer: Granny: I have kept a house in a gale for decades and a ferry timetable in my head for longer. A business is small beer, dear.
Granny: Off you walk, {player}. I will mind it and I will mind the door, and nobody will stand where the ferry goes.
chat: Granny: The first rule of Oban is do not stand where the ferry is about to go. People forget, regularly.
Granny: Madainn mhath, that is good morning. Say it back wrongly, I shall be delighted.
Granny: Bring a coat. That is the second rule. I will not say it again until I do.
thanks: Granny weighs the bag of queenies as if it held the crown jewels.
Granny: Queenies! Fresh, I can tell by the smell. Thank you, dear. That is the ferry and the supper sorted.

regulars.name: Ewen MacMillan
regulars.hint: Ewen says a bowl of Scotch broth is what a person should be handed after a day on the hill, and not one minute before.
intro: Ewen: Ewen MacMillan. Mountain rescue, on the quiet days. Before you ask, yes, I will ask where you are going. I ask everyone.
Ewen: A bowl of Scotch broth, hot, after a day up the Ben, is about the best thing there is. If you ever have one going spare, I will count it as a green place.
meet: Ewen is on the esplanade at Oban with a flask, looking at the sea the way he would look at a hill he did not trust.
Ewen: A day off. I told my wife where I was going and when I would be back, as I always do. She says that is not a hobby, it is a condition.
Ewen: Mòran taing for stopping, that is many thanks. Tell someone where you are headed next. I will know if you do not.
letter: The Ben had its hat on all week, so I stayed down and fixed the gate, and the snowhares stayed up and kept their own counsel. Tell someone where you are going. Always.
offer: Ewen: Your business, {player}. I have spent years looking after people who did not plan the day, so a plan I can manage.
Ewen: Off you go. I will keep an eye on it, and I will want to know what time you are back.
chat: Ewen: Snowhares go white in winter. Up on the Ben it is a decent trick, and it still works on most people.
Ewen: The forecast said fine. The Ben said otherwise. I go with the Ben.
Ewen: Mountain rescue are up the hill a lot. If you are going up, tell someone. I will keep saying it.
thanks: Ewen takes the broth in both hands and has a careful sip, like a man checking a path.
Ewen: That is a proper broth. Barley and all. Mòran taing, {player}. And well done for telling me you were coming.

regulars.name: Gethin Hughes
regulars.hint: Gethin says a bowl of proper home-made cawl is the only thing that has ever made him close a book and eat at the table.
intro: Gethin: Gethin. I am revising. By which I mean I am sitting near a book, and the book is winning.
Gethin: Mam makes cawl on Sundays and it is better on Monday. If you ever have some home-made cawl, I will say diolch like I mean it, because I will.
meet: Gethin is by the ferry terminal in Dublin with a rucksack and a very tired face, watching the boats as if they might take him back by themselves.
Gethin: Over on the ferry for a look at the university. The Romans picked Holyhead for the harbour and I picked this for the pizza. Both fine decisions.
Gethin: Bore da, that is good morning, which it is, technically. Do not tell Mam I am not at the library.
letter: The revision is going. I keep saying it, and Mam keeps saying 'is it', and Nan says she saw a selklet on the rocks again, which she did not. Probably. She is usually right about animals.
offer: Gethin: A business is a good idea, {player}. It is a lot more fun than anything with an exam in it.
Gethin: I will keep an eye on it. I will do it at the table, so I can say I am working.
chat: Gethin: The old fort at Holyhead sits over the harbour for a reason. Same reason there is a ferry. I did learn something.
Gethin: Nan says there is a selklet on the rocks. Nan is right about animals and wrong about directions.
Gethin: Exams soon. I am calm. I am calm in the way of a lad about to be very busy.
thanks: Gethin lifts the lid of the pot, breathes in, and forgets the book entirely.
Gethin: Cawl! Diolch, {player}. That is Monday sorted and Mam will say it was her idea.

regulars.name: Gareth Lloyd
regulars.hint: Gareth says a good perch off the canal bank is the nearest thing to a perfect afternoon, and he would not argue with you about it.
intro: Gareth: Ahoy. Gareth Lloyd. Well, ahoy if you live on the canal. I live on land. Mostly.
Gareth: I own seven windlasses and can find one on a good day. A perch off the towpath, now, I can always find a place for. Bring me one and I will count it as a green place.
meet: Gareth is on the Chester canal side, watching a boat go through a lock with his arms folded and his whole body leaning in to help.
Gareth: A day out for the boats. I came to watch somebody else do the paddles for once. It is not relaxing, it is supervising.
Gareth: Diolch for stopping. Mind the lock edge. That is the advice and the whole of it.
letter: The canal was quiet, so I walked the towpath and looked at the water, and an elverlet crossed the meadow so quickly I could not have said what it was. Unimpressed, as ever. A windlass has turned up in the shed. That makes eight, or the same one twice.
offer: Gareth: A business, {player}. I have kept a lock in a hurry before now. A small business I can keep at a steady pace.
Gareth: Off you go. I will mind it, and I will find a windlass in a minute, I promise.
chat: Gareth: A windlass winds the paddle on a lock. People ask. I tell them. Some of them even nod.
Gareth: Elverlets in the water meadows. Very fast, very unimpressed. I admire them.
Gareth: The kettle is quiet. That is worrying. Come in and we shall sort it out.
thanks: Gareth holds the perch up to the light and inspects it like a man checking a lock gate.
Gareth: A proper fish. Diolch, {player}. That will do for tea, and for the story, which will get bigger.

regulars.name: Peigi MacKinnon
regulars.hint: Peigi says a mackerel grilled the same evening it is landed is a better supper than anything the shops of Inverness could offer.
intro: Peigi: Fàilte. Peigi MacKinnon. Sit in by the stove, you look like you have walked.
Peigi: A mackerel, grilled the day it comes out of the sea, is the best supper there is. If you have one to spare, I will count it as a green place.
meet: Peigi is in Inverness by the river, in a good coat, looking at the bridges as if checking they are all still there.
Peigi: I came over to the town for a day. There is a lot of it, and all of it in a hurry. I miss the loch already.
Peigi: Madainn mhath, that is good morning. I will not make you say it back, but I will notice if you do.
letter: The loch has been quiet and I have not minded. The Cuillin had snow on top, and an orcalet showed off the point on Tuesday. I did not mistake it for a seal. It would have sulked.
offer: Peigi: A business, {player}? I have kept a croft house through a good few storms. A wee business is easy by comparison.
Peigi: Away you go and see the world. I will keep it tidy, and the stove will be on.
chat: Peigi: The Cuillin is made of rough black rock. It grips boots wonderfully and shreds knees even better.
Peigi: Orcalets off the point on a calm day. Bring binoculars, and do not mistake a seal for one.
Peigi: Nothing happened on the loch today. It was lovely. I recommend it.
thanks: Peigi turns the mackerel over, sniffs it once, and smiles like she has been told good news.
Peigi: Mòran taing, {player}. That is the supper sorted, and the stove will be glad of it.
